questions.title: Choosing the first intervention when failure types are mixed
questions.prompt:
An insurer evaluates its OpenAI Responses API support assistant on 200 questions; 48 fail:

- 31: It does not know recently revised clauses in monthly updated policy terms, or answers using old clauses.
- 12: It omits a required notice at the end of the answer.
- 5: It misunderstands the question's intent.

Only one change fits this sprint. It must directly address the largest failure group, reflect revised terms by the next day without human intervention, and permit before/after comparison on the same evaluation set. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Perform supervised fine-tuning on 2,000 Q&A pairs reflecting revised terms and compare before/after on the same evaluation set.
Add three answer examples containing the required notice to the system prompt and compare before/after on the same evaluation set.
Upload policy files to a vector store, attach `file_search`, and separately score retrieval results and answers on the same evaluation set.
Have staff manually paste revised-clause summaries into the system prompt monthly and compare before/after on the same evaluation set.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answer: {{option:C}}**

The decisive facts are the largest group—31 revised-policy failures—and automatic incorporation by the next day. OpenAI's accuracy-optimization guide distinguishes context optimization, such as RAG, for missing/outdated knowledge from LLM optimization, such as few-shot examples or fine-tuning, for format/tone inconsistency. These 31 failures are knowledge gaps. `file_search` retrieves vector-store files into context, so an automated pipeline can replace revised files. RAG can fail during retrieval or when the model misuses correct context, so score retrieved results and answers separately to locate the cause.

- {{option:A}} embeds knowledge in weights and needs retraining after each revision, failing automatic next-day updates. The deprecation documentation also says even existing active customers cannot create new fine-tuning jobs from January 6, 2027.
- {{option:B}} appropriately targets the 12 formatting failures but not the largest group of 31.
- {{option:C}} targets the knowledge gap, automatically reflects revisions and supports comparison. Tradeoffs are a new retrieval-miss failure point and leaving the 12 missing-notice failures unresolved.
- {{option:D}} targets the right context gap but depends on manual work, violating the no-human-intervention condition.

The guide permits combining tuning and RAG, but also describes a case where adding RAG to an already tuned model added noise and reduced scores. This is why every change needs evaluation.

**References**: [Optimizing LLM accuracy › LLM optimization context](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/optimizing-llm-accuracy) · [File search](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-file-search) · [Deprecations › Update to OpenAI's self-serve fine-tuning](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/deprecations)

questions.title: Improve Gemini API classification without tuning
questions.prompt:
A team classifies inquiries into 40 categories with Gemini API. Zero-shot accuracy misses the target, and 3,000 labeled historical inquiries are available. Constraints:

- Stay **within Gemini API**, with no new platform or migration.
- Classify immediately in **real time**.
- **Minimize added input tokens per request**.
- Category definitions change quarterly and must update **within one day without retraining**.

What is most appropriate?

options.text: Tune on the 3,000 labels in Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, use short prompts, and retune when definitions change.
Include all 3,000 labeled examples in system instructions on every request, editing them when definitions change.
Batch inquiries at half standard price and spend the savings on a larger model with more examples.
Pre-embed labeled examples with gemini-embedding-2 and include only a few nearest examples as few-shot context for each new inquiry.

questions.explanation:
The key constraints are staying within Gemini API, minimal input growth, and updates without retraining. Documentation says Gemini API and AI Studio currently have no tunable models and directs tuning to Agent Platform, so this task must use prompts and embeddings. Prompt guidance recommends few-shot examples but warns that too many may cause overfitting. Embedding guidance describes symmetric classification prefixes for gemini-embedding-2. Combining them retrieves only similar examples, limits tokens, and requires re-embedding only changed examples when definitions change.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: violates constraints)**: It follows the documented tuning route but requires platform migration and quarterly retuning.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Input tokens increase substantially, with the documented overfitting risk from excessive examples.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Batch targets a 24-hour turnaround for nonurgent work. It violates real time and does not use the labels.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: It uses labeled data while meeting all four constraints.

Also note: gemini-embedding-2 does not accept task_type. For the same task with gemini-embedding-001, use task_type CLASSIFICATION.

**References**: [Fine-tuning with the Gemini API](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/model-tuning) · [Prompt design strategies › Zero-shot vs few-shot prompts](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies) · [Embeddings › Task types with Embeddings 2](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/embeddings) · [Batch API › Technical details](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/batch-api)

questions.title: Design support responses for a new OpenAI organization without fine-tuning
questions.prompt:
A startup created its OpenAI API organization in September 2026 and is building product-manual support responses. It initially planned fine-tuning to teach manuals and fix response format. Requirements:

- Responses must obey a **fixed JSON Schema** consumed downstream.
- Manuals total about **400,000 tokens**, change **weekly**, and updates must affect answers the next day.
- Every request must have **at most 30,000 input tokens, including cached tokens**.
- Retain **OpenAI as the sole vendor**, with **no extra operations staff**.

Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Upload manuals to a vector store, limit file_search with max_num_results, and use Structured Outputs with json_schema and strict: true.
Put all manuals at the beginning of every prompt for caching and use Structured Outputs with json_schema and strict: true.
Use an affiliated company's existing fine-tuning organization to run weekly SFT on manual Q&A pairs, with strict Structured Outputs.
Upload manuals to a vector store, limit file_search with max_num_results, and use text.format json_object (JSON mode).

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are fixed schema, 400k tokens with weekly changes, a 30k input limit, and a single vendor with no additional staff. Each blocks a different route, so knowledge and formatting must be assessed together. Only Structured Outputs guarantees schema adherence. OpenAI-managed file search handles changing large manuals within the token budget without separate search infrastructure. Reducing max_num_results lowers tokens and latency but may hurt quality, so even the correct design trades off retrieval omissions and needs evaluation.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It meets all four constraints. Evaluate retrieval omissions separately after reducing result count.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Schema, freshness, and vendor requirements are met, but all 400k tokens remain input even on cache hits, far exceeding 30k.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Schema and input limits are met, but changing knowledge requires weekly retraining. Deprecation guidance says even existing active customers cannot create new tuning jobs from 2027-01-06, and tuned models follow their base-model retirement. Weekly retraining therefore stops early next year and adds pipeline operations.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: confusing similar features)**: Retrieval, token, and vendor conditions match {{option:A}}, but JSON mode guarantees valid JSON, not schema adherence.

Also note: This organization was created after 2026-05-07 and has never fine-tuned, so it cannot create fine-tuning jobs in its own organization.

**References**: [Deprecations › Update to OpenAI's self-serve fine-tuning](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/deprecations) · [Structured model outputs › Structured Outputs vs JSON mode](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs) · [File search › Limiting the number of results](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-file-search)

questions.title: Claude prompt placement for policy Q&A with per-user information
questions.prompt: An internal policy Q&A team uses the Claude API. Its approximately 150,000-token handbook changes quarterly, while dozens of questions arrive each minute during working hours. Applicability depends on role and department, so each request includes the questioner's department and grade. Most observed failures miss exception clauses in the handbook's middle. Requirements are lower latency/cost for repeated requests, minimal implementation/operations burden, and answers grounded in the full handbook with fewer missed middle clauses. Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Chunk the handbook, add contextual descriptions, build embedding/BM25 hybrid retrieval, rerank and send the top 20 chunks with the question, and require relevant-chunk citations first.
Put user details and the question first, then the full handbook with `cache_control` on its last block, and require relevant-clause citations first.
Split the handbook into four chapter blocks with `cache_control` on each, send only chapters matching the question type, and require relevant-clause citations first.
Put the full handbook first with `cache_control` at its end, then user details and the question, and require relevant-clause citations first.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answer: {{option:D}}**

The decisive facts are per-request user changes, latency/cost and missed middle clauses. Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval article says knowledge bases below 200,000 tokens can be included in full with prompt caching, without retrieval. Caching hashes the prefix in tools → system → messages order: any changed block before the breakpoint prevents a hit. The fixed handbook must therefore precede changing user details. Prompting guidance also says long documents first and questions last can improve quality by up to 30%. All options request citations, so evidence scope and cache-prefix placement distinguish them.

- {{option:A}} reduces retrieval failure in large knowledge bases but adds unnecessary implementation/operations burden here and grounds answers in only selected chunks rather than the full handbook.
- {{option:B}} preserves full evidence, but changing user information before the breakpoint changes every prefix and prevents cache hits. Question-before-document placement also reverses the recommendation.
- {{option:C}} uses a real capability—up to four breakpoints—but selected chapters omit full-handbook coverage. Omitting earlier chapters changes the prefix and lowers hit rates, while classification logic adds maintenance.
- {{option:D}} caches the fixed handbook and puts variable details/questions last. Its tradeoffs are including the full handbook in every request and paying cache-write/rewrite costs after expiry.

**References**: [Introducing Contextual Retrieval](https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval) · [Prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) · [Prompting best practices › Long context prompting](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices)

questions.title: Target the two largest groups of retrieval-augmented failures
questions.prompt:
A policy Q&A team uses OpenAI Responses API file_search with gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14 and is an existing customer that has recently used fine-tuning. It inspects 60 failures among 300 evaluation questions, including retrieval results through include: file_search_call.results:

- 33: The needed clause was retrieved, but the answer applied it incorrectly.
- 19: A similar clause from another division ranked above the correct clause, and the answer mixed them.
- 8: The needed clause was not retrieved.

A preliminary test with four clause-application examples fixed some of the 33 failures. Constraints:

- The solution must **operate beyond 2027**.
- This sprint must **target each of the two largest failure groups**.
- Files can have division attributes, and the questioner's division is known at request time.

Choose **TWO** actions.

options.text: Clarify how to apply retrieved clauses in instructions and adopt the successful examples as formal few-shot examples.
Increase max_num_results to retrieve more clauses and reduce omissions.
Since examples helped, SFT the current model with training examples including retrieval results.
Reduce max_num_results to keep only top clauses, reducing context noise and tokens.
Add division attributes to policy files and use filters to retain only the questioner's division.

questions.explanation:
The decisive facts are the failure breakdown, the two-largest-groups requirement, and operation beyond 2027. OpenAI distinguishes retrieval failures, such as wrong or excessive irrelevant context, from LLM failures despite correct context. The 33 cases need prompt improvements; the 19 need irrelevant-context filtering. The accuracy guide recommends fine-tuning when few-shot works, but deprecation documentation blocks that route for this team's lifespan requirement.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It targets the 33 incorrect applications of correct context at the prompt layer.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: It targets the smallest eight-case group and can worsen the 19 cases by adding irrelevant clauses.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: It follows the guide's sequence and advice to train on RAG examples, but even active customers cannot create jobs from 2027-01-06. gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14 and its tuned versions retire on 2027-01-14, violating continued operation.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: confusing similar features)**: Result limits reduce noise generally, but wrong-division clauses rank above the correct ones here, so truncation removes correct clauses first. Documentation warns result limits can reduce quality.
- **{{option:E}} (Correct)**: Division filters remove the cause of the 19 cases regardless of ranking.

**References**: [Optimizing LLM accuracy › Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/optimizing-llm-accuracy) · [File search › Retrieval customization](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-file-search) · [Deprecations › Update to OpenAI's self-serve fine-tuning](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/deprecations) · [Deprecations › 2026-10-14: GPT-4 series model deprecations](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/deprecations)

questions.title: Design an OpenAI embedding index under memory, budget, and accuracy constraints
questions.prompt:
A search team will index 12 million chunks with OpenAI embeddings. Constraints:

- **40 GB** for vectors, float32 at four bytes per value.
- Embedding cost at most **four times processing the corpus with synchronous text-embedding-3-small**.
- The vector database assumes unit vectors and uses **dot-product similarity**.
- Completion is not urgent; **maximize retrieval accuracy** within these constraints.

The model table lists 62,500 pages per dollar for text-embedding-3-small and 9,615 for text-embedding-3-large. What is most appropriate?

options.text: Use text-embedding-3-large with dimensions 768, submitting partitioned Batch API jobs.
Use text-embedding-3-large with dimensions 1024, submitting partitioned Batch API jobs.
Obtain 3072-dimensional large vectors through Batch, truncate to the first 768 values, and store unchanged.
Use large with dimensions 768 through parallel synchronous API calls to finish within days.

questions.explanation:
All four constraints require combining embedding and Batch documentation. Memory is 12 million × 768 × 4 bytes ≈ 36.9 GB, while 1024 dimensions need about 49.2 GB. Large costs about 6.5 times small (62,500 ÷ 9,615), but Batch's 50% discount reduces this to about 3.25 times, within budget. The guide recommends dimensions for v3 shortening and renormalization after manual truncation.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It uses the stronger model while meeting memory, budget, and dot-product requirements. The tradeoff is operational management of roughly 240 batches because each allows at most 50,000 embedding inputs, and asynchronous results arrive within 24 hours per batch, delaying completion.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Cost and accuracy are suitable, but approximately 49.2 GB exceeds memory.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Memory and cost match {{option:A}}, but truncated vectors are not unit length, distorting dot-product rankings. Renormalization is required.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Memory and accuracy match {{option:A}} and it finishes faster, but synchronous cost is about 6.5 times small, exceeding budget. Nonurgent completion does not justify this cost.

Also note: Large reduced to 256 dimensions still exceeds unreduced text-embedding-ada-002 on MTEB.

**References**: [Vector embeddings › Embedding models](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/embeddings) · [Vector embeddings › Reducing embedding dimensions](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/embeddings) · [Batch API](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/batch)

questions.title: Page-level gemini-embedding-2 indexing for 40-page PDF manuals
questions.prompt: A team building Gemini API search over internal equipment manuals, approximately 40 pages per PDF, uses `gemini-embedding-2`. Users submit text questions embedded with the documented retrieval prefix. No page may be truncated from embedding input, results must be page-level with one vector per page, and embedding cost must be minimized even if indexing takes days. Which indexing method is most appropriate?

options.text: Send each entire manual PDF in one request through the Batch API, producing one vector per document.
Split manuals into six-page PDFs and process through Batch, producing one vector per six-page group.
Split manuals into single-page PDFs and submit each file as a separate Batch API request, producing one vector per page.
Split manuals into single-page PDFs and call the synchronous API in parallel, producing one vector per page.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answer: {{option:C}}**

The constraints are no truncation, page-level vectors, and minimum cost without latency pressure. Gemini documentation says `gemini-embedding-2` accepts one PDF per request, up to six pages, within an 8,192-token total limit including 258 visual tokens per page plus extracted text. Excess input is silently truncated. It recommends one page per PDF for best quality, and Batch costs 50% of the standard embedding price.

- {{option:A}} silently loses pages beyond the six-page limit and does not produce page-level vectors.
- {{option:B}} avoids page-limit truncation and lowers cost but produces six-page-group vectors rather than page-level results.
- {{option:C}} sends separate single-page requests, avoids truncation, yields per-page vectors and halves embedding cost through Batch. Tradeoffs are approximately 40 times as many vectors per document, greater storage/search costs, and no guaranteed completion time.
- {{option:D}} produces the same result shape as {{option:C}} but pays twice as much for synchronous processing when speed is unnecessary.

Multiple inputs in one request's `contents` produce one aggregated embedding. For separate vectors, wrap inputs in separate `Content` objects or use the Batch API.

**References**: [Embeddings › Multimodal embeddings with Embeddings 2](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/embeddings) · [Embeddings › Batch embeddings](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/embeddings)

questions.title: Improve Voyage retrieval when chunks lose document context
questions.prompt:
A Claude API product-manual RAG team uses Voyage AI embeddings recommended by Anthropic. Most failures involve chunks such as "How to reset this device" whose product name appears only in an earlier chapter. Constraints:

- Manuals average **60,000 tokens** each.
- Add **no per-chunk LLM calls** to indexing because of preprocessing cost and operations.
- The query p95 latency budget is exhausted, so **no additional query-time stage** is allowed.
- Vectors must have **at most 512 dimensions**.

Choose **TWO** actions to apply together.

options.text: Use Claude to generate context for every chunk, reducing cost with prompt caching, then embed with voyage-4-large at 512 dimensions.
Rerank the first-stage top 100 using latency/cost-optimized rerank-3-lite, passing only 20 to Claude.
Pass whole manuals to voyage-context-4 contextualized_embed() with enable_auto_chunking enabled.
Set voyage-context-4 output dimensions to its supported 512 instead of default 1024.
Prechunk manuals into per-document lists for contextualized_embed(), disable automatic chunking, and manage boundaries manually.

questions.explanation:
All four constraints matter. Anthropic says voyage-context-4 creates chunk vectors containing whole-document context without manual metadata enrichment, supporting 256, 512, 1024 (default), and 2048 dimensions. Its 120,000-token limit applies only with enable_auto_chunking; without it, total tokens across inputs cannot exceed 32,000. Contextual Retrieval is effective but generates context through a Claude call for each chunk.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: It is a proven retrieval improvement and meets dimensions, but adds per-chunk LLM calls.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Even a lightweight reranker adds a query-time call. It also cannot rescue a context-poor chunk absent from first-stage results.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It embeds document context at indexing time without LLM calls and handles 60k-token manuals through automatic chunking.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: A supported dimension meets storage limits.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Disabling automatic chunking limits total input to 32,000 tokens, so an average 60k-token manual cannot be passed at once.

Also note: Voyage embeddings are unit-normalized, making dot product and cosine similarity equivalent.

**References**: [Embeddings › Contextualized chunk models](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/embeddings) · [Embeddings › Rerankers](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/embeddings) · [Introducing Contextual Retrieval](https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval)

questions.title: Migrating the embedding model for a five-million-document index
questions.prompt:
A team indexed five million text documents using Gemini API `gemini-embedding-001` at the default 3072 float32 dimensions. Next quarter it will launch similarity search using user-uploaded PDFs or images to search existing text documents and PDFs together.

- Meet next quarter's launch.
- Reindexing must cost no more than 60% of processing everything with the synchronous embedding API, and be minimized within that limit; it may take days.
- Keep existing text search uninterrupted during migration.
- Combined old/new indexes during migration must fit within 1.3 times the current index size.

Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Keep the 001 index and separately index only images/PDFs with `gemini-embedding-2` at 768 dimensions. Search both indexes and merge rankings for each query, evaluate merged results, then launch.
Use Batch to re-embed all documents in chunks into a new `gemini-embedding-2` 768-dimensional index while serving the old index. Evaluate queries, then switch them to the new index.
Use parallel synchronous calls to re-embed all documents into a new `gemini-embedding-2` 768-dimensional index for schedule margin while serving the old one. Evaluate queries, then switch.
Use Batch to re-embed all documents in chunks into a new `gemini-embedding-2` 1024-dimensional index while serving the old one. Evaluate queries, then switch.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answer: {{option:B}}**

The decisive conditions are searching existing text with PDF/image queries, the 60% budget, 1.3-times capacity, and uninterrupted service. The two models' embedding spaces are incompatible, so migration requires full re-embedding. `gemini-embedding-001` is text-only; `gemini-embedding-2` accepts PDFs/images. Existing documents must also be in the latter space for PDF queries to find them. Batch costs 50% of standard pricing, within the 60% budget; synchronous processing costs 100%. Current capacity is 5 million × 3072 × 4 bytes ≈ 61.4 GB. A 768-dimensional index is about 15.4 GB, or 25%, for a combined 1.25 times; 1024 dimensions is about 20.5 GB, or 33%, for approximately 1.33 times.

- {{option:A}} is cheapest and timely but cannot compare incompatible vectors to find existing text from PDF queries; ranking fusion does not solve this.
- {{option:B}} meets all four. Tradeoffs are much greater reindexing cost than {{option:A}}—minimal within the feasible budget but not zero—holding both indexes during transition, and splitting large Batch submissions because jobs expire if unfinished after 48 hours.
- {{option:C}} has the same scope/capacity as {{option:B}} but costs 100%, exceeding 60%. Speed does not justify this when days are acceptable.
- {{option:D}} meets budget but its approximately 1.33-times capacity exceeds 1.3. The documentation lists 768 as a recommended dimension.

`gemini-embedding-2` automatically normalizes reduced dimensions; `gemini-embedding-001` requires manual normalization for dimensions other than 3072.

**References**: [Embeddings › Migration from gemini-embedding-001](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/embeddings) · [Embeddings › Batch embeddings](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/embeddings) · [Embeddings › Controlling embedding size](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/embeddings)

questions.title: Constructing tone-training data from pairwise preferences
questions.prompt: A team is preparing tuning data to align chat-response tone with its brand, without yet choosing a platform. It has 4,000 single-turn comparisons where agents selected the better of two responses to the same question, plus 300 exemplary responses edited by brand staff. Use both signals, never train the rejected response as an imitation target, and leave preference learning as the final training stage. Based on OpenAI's tuning-method documentation, which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Extract only preferred responses, combine them with 300 exemplars, and run SFT once on the 4,300 examples.
First train DPO on 4,000 single-turn pairs, then finish tone with SFT on the 300 exemplars.
Use both preferred and rejected responses as SFT targets, combining them with exemplars for 8,300 examples.
First run SFT on the 300 exemplars, then use that model as the starting point for DPO on the 4,000 single-turn pairs.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answer: {{option:D}}**

The three requirements and single-turn comparison/exemplar data determine the choice. OpenAI's DPO guide targets subjective tasks such as tone/style. Each example contains `input`, `preferred_output` and `non_preferred_output` and must be single-turn. It recommends SFT on a subset of high-quality preferred responses before DPO. That order uses exemplars through SFT, comparisons through DPO, and finishes with preference learning.

- {{option:A}} works technically but discards the rejected contrast that expresses which response is better, failing to preserve both signals.
- {{option:B}} uses both datasets but reverses the order; final SFT may overwrite DPO preference effects and contradicts the recommended SFT-then-DPO sequence.
- {{option:C}} treats rejected responses as correct targets, teaching undesirable tone and violating data-quality principles.
- {{option:D}} satisfies all three, at the cost of two training jobs and additional time/expense.

Even existing active OpenAI customers cannot create new fine-tuning jobs from January 6, 2027. The DPO-supported `gpt-4.1` family retires January 14, 2027, with nano retiring October 23, 2026. Preparing this data form without tying it to one platform is therefore prudent.

**References**: [Direct preference optimization › Data format](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/direct-preference-optimization) · [Direct preference optimization › Use SFT and DPO together](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/direct-preference-optimization) · [Deprecations › Update to OpenAI's self-serve fine-tuning](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/deprecations)

questions.title: Selecting two feasible tuning plans
questions.prompt: Today is October 17, 2026. An ML team that is an existing active OpenAI customer submits five tuning plans. Every tuned model must operate through the end of December 2026, and training starts during November. Which TWO plans meet both OpenAI's method/data requirements and retirement schedule?

options.text: Security-policy violation classification with high expert agreement, automated grading and partial success by the current model: RFT on `o4-mini-2025-04-16` using grader rewards.
Inquiry-type classification with one correct label per input: SFT on `gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14` using input/correct-label examples.
Support-response tone matching with four preceding conversation turns in each input: DPO on `gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14` using preferred/rejected final-response pairs.
Emphasizing key points in long-report summaries with text input/output: single-turn better/worse summary pairs for DPO on `gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14`.
Classifying defect reports with attached photos: DPO on `gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14` using good/bad response pairs for the same input.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answers: {{option:B}}, {{option:D}}**

Method, data shape, model ID and operation through December all matter. OpenAI associates SFT with classification/specific formats, DPO with focused summaries and tone/style, and RFT with complex domain reasoning. DPO supports only text input/output and one turn per example. RFT requires expert agreement, gradability and a model already succeeding to some extent. `o4-mini-2025-04-16` retires October 23, 2026; `gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14` and tuned variants retire January 14, 2027.

- {{option:A}} meets RFT task conditions but its base model retires well before December ends.
- {{option:B}} is a standard SFT classification use case and the model remains available until January 14, 2027.
- {{option:C}} is a suitable DPO task but four-turn context violates its single-turn data requirement.
- {{option:D}} is a documented DPO use case with single-turn text data and adequate model lifetime.
- {{option:E}} violates text-only DPO input requirements through images.

Even {{option:B}} and {{option:D}} require existing active customers to create jobs before January 6, 2027. Tuned models follow base-model retirement schedules; method suitability and actual availability must be checked separately.

**References**: [Model optimization › Fine-tuning methods](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/model-optimization) · [Reinforcement fine-tuning › When should I use reinforcement fine-tuning?](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reinforcement-fine-tuning) · [Direct preference optimization](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/direct-preference-optimization) · [Deprecations › 2026-04-22: Legacy GPT model snapshots](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/deprecations) · [Deprecations › 2026-10-14: GPT-4 series model deprecations](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/deprecations)

questions.title: When a task suits RFT but model lifetime blocks the plan
questions.prompt:
A security team that has recently used OpenAI fine-tuning wants better judgments of whether code changes violate security policy. Experts generally agree, automatic grading is possible, and current `o4-mini` succeeds only on some cases. Experiments on the same 500-case holdout show:

- `o4-mini-2025-04-16`: current prompt 71%, trial RFT 93%.
- `gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14`: trial SFT 92%.
- The recommended `o4-mini` replacement: 12-example prompt 86%, three-example prompt 83%.

Monthly inference costs are 1.8 times current for 12 examples, 1.2 times for three examples, and 0.6 times for SFT. questions.prompt: Pre-deployment review of a customer-support SFT model finds (1) excessive 'I cannot help' refusals for valid requests and (2) fabricated order details absent from the conversation. Inspection of 3,000 training examples finds 58% refusals versus an expected operational 6%, 14% unsupported-information responses (about 420), and 92% annotator agreement. options.text: Shorten instructions in every example to reduce training cost, leaving response composition unchanged.
Increase epochs by one or two to make the model follow training exemplars more closely.
Reduce refusal examples to bring their proportion closer to the expected operational distribution.
Find every annotator disagreement, unify criteria and relabel them all.
Find responses containing information absent from earlier conversation and correct or remove them.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answers: {{option:C}}, {{option:E}}**

The symptoms, measured proportions, direct-cause requirement and 500-example budget matter. OpenAI's tuning guidance recommends matching response-type distributions to inference needs—for example, 60% refusals when only 5% are expected predicts excessive refusal—and ensuring responses are supported by preceding conversation, otherwise fabrication is learned. The 58% versus 6% mismatch explains symptom (1), and the 14% unsupported responses explain (2); 420 fits within 500.

- {{option:A}} reduces cost but contradicts advice to retain previously effective instructions in every example and targets neither cause.
- {{option:B}} is for insufficient imitation of training data; imitating biased data more closely may worsen both symptoms.
- {{option:C}} targets excessive refusal without consuming manual rewrite budget, at the cost of less data.

questions.title: Use break-even accuracy to assess base and tuned models
questions.prompt:
A support-automation team assigns business value following OpenAI's accuracy guide:

- AI resolves an inquiry immediately: +$10.
- When AI is wrong, 90% cause unnecessary human escalation (−$20) and 10% cause churn (−$500).

Three candidates:

- (1) Base model + improved prompt: 85% holdout accuracy.
- (2) Tuned model: 93% training accuracy, 86% holdout accuracy.
- (3) Base model + retrieval augmentation: 89% holdout accuracy.

Only candidates with **nonnegative expected profit** may launch. Which break-even accuracy and launch choices are correct?

options.text: About 87%; (2) and (3).
About 87%; only (3).
About 82%; all three.
About 98%; none.

questions.explanation:
The outcome values, nonnegative-profit threshold, and candidate (2)'s two scores are decisive. With accuracy p, expected profit per inquiry is 10p − (1 − p)(0.9 × 20 + 0.1 × 500) = 10p − 68(1 − p). Break-even is p = 68 ÷ 78 ≈ 87.2%. SFT guidance requires evaluation on a holdout reserved before training, so only holdout scores count.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Candidate (2)'s 93% is training accuracy, not generalization. Its 86% holdout score misses break-even.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Only candidate (3), at 89% holdout accuracy, qualifies.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: 81.5% is the guide's example with different monetary assumptions. Recalculate using this team's values.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: This treats all errors as $500 churn, although 90% incur only escalation cost.

questions.title: Sequence a base-versus-tuned model evaluation
questions.prompt:
A team is deciding whether to retain a base model with an improved prompt or replace it with a tuned model. Classification labels will use exact-match grading; free-text tone will use an LLM grader. Each step consumes artifacts from earlier steps. Put them in dependency order.

- (1) Run the base model with the current prompt across the full holdout using the validated grader, obtaining baseline scores and failures.
- (2) Separate failures into missing knowledge and inconsistent format/behavior; if behavior dominates, decide the response-type mix for tuning data.
- (3) Sample production logs, obtain expert labels, exclude these samples from candidate training data, and freeze them as a holdout.
- (4) Compare LLM-grader judgments with expert labels on part of the holdout to check consistent agreement.
- (5) Evaluate the model tuned on the chosen mix using the same holdout and grader, and compare against the baseline.

items.text: Run the base model with the current prompt across the full holdout using the validated grader, obtaining baseline scores and failures.
Separate failures into missing knowledge and inconsistent format/behavior; if behavior dominates, decide the response-type mix for tuning data.
Sample production logs, obtain expert labels, exclude these samples from candidate training data, and freeze them as a holdout.
Compare LLM-grader judgments with expert labels on part of the holdout to check consistent agreement.
Evaluate the model tuned on the chosen mix using the same holdout and grader, and compare against the baseline.

questions.explanation:
Artifact dependencies determine the order. Expert labels are needed to validate the grader; a validated grader makes the baseline trustworthy; baseline failures determine whether to tune and how to compose data; and the resulting model is needed for comparison. OpenAI evaluation guidance says to scale LLM judges once they consistently agree with human labels. Accuracy guidance establishes a baseline, then separates context and behavior failures to choose the next step. SFT guidance reserves holdout data before training.

| Order | Step | Dependency | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | (3) Freeze holdout and expert labels | Starting point: create evaluation data separate from training and human labels | Supervised fine-tuning: Evaluate the result; Evaluation best practices: Collect dataset |
| 2 | (4) Validate the grader | Requires expert labels from (3) | Evaluation best practices: Create and combine different types of evaluators |
| 3 | (1) Baseline and failure list | The grader validated in (4) makes scores trustworthy | Optimizing LLM accuracy: LLM optimization context |
| 4 | (2) Diagnose route and data mix | Uses failures from (1) | LLM optimization context; Fine-tuning best practices: Iterating on data quality |
| 5 | (5) Compare tuned model | Requires the model from (2) and baseline from (1) | Supervised fine-tuning: Evaluate the result |

Also note: A common mistake is running (1) first and checking the grader only if results look strange, after an unvalidated score has already determined whether to tune. Step (5) requires a new OpenAI training job, unavailable even to active customers from 2027-01-06. The same sequence applies on other tuning platforms.

questions.prompt: A team compares support responses from a base model averaging 180 words and a tuned model averaging 70. An LLM judge compares responses to the same questions and gives the base model a 64% win rate. Agreement with 100 expert-labeled cases is 71%, and the judge is the same model as the base candidate. The expert budget covers 300 response ratings. Mark each statement Yes if it matches OpenAI/Anthropic evaluation guidance, otherwise No.

items.text: Spending the entire 300-rating budget on direct expert scoring rather than maximizing evaluation cases is more conducive to a reliable decision under the documentation's principles.
The 64% win rate may contain verbosity bias, so controlling response length and comparing again aligns with the guidance.
Using the same model as both judge and base candidate is consistent with Anthropic's best practices once 71% agreement is verified.
To improve 71% agreement, first test the most capable judge and more specific criteria before switching to a smaller judge for cost savings.

**Answers: 1 No, 2 Yes, 3 No, 4 Yes**

Anthropic favors many automatically graded cases over a small manually graded set even if the signal is slightly weaker, recommends avoiding human grading where possible, and testing LLM-grader reliability before scaling. A code-example comment identifies using a different judge from the generation model as general best practice. OpenAI describes verbosity and position bias, recommends length controls and reasoning before scoring, and says to start with the most capable judge and establish human-label agreement before optimizing cost/latency.

1. **No:** This reverses the principle. Spending all 300 on direct human grading limits coverage; human grading is slow/expensive. Expand automated coverage and use experts to validate the judge.
2. **Yes:** Base responses are over 2.5 times longer, so verbosity bias may inflate wins; length controls are recommended.
3. **No:** Regardless of measured agreement, using a different judging model is the documented best practice.
4. **Yes:** First improve agreement with a capable model and clear, detailed criteria, then optimize cost/latency.

A document-classification team is choosing between a tuned small model with a short prompt and a large base model with a long prompt containing 20 examples. Each response contains a label and one sentence explaining the classification for a reviewer. Conditions:

- 4,000 production-log cases have confirmed labels and are holdouts unused by either model. Explanation quality has no labels.
- Expert grading budget: **300 cases**. Decision deadline: **two weeks**.
- Requirements: label accuracy at least current performance, **p95 latency at most 1.5 seconds**, a **monthly inference-cost cap**, and preserved explanation quality.

Which experiment is most appropriate?

options.text: Spend all 300 expert judgments directly on candidate responses, evaluate labels and explanations on those 300, and measure latency/cost with production configurations.
Exact-match all 4,000 labels, use an LLM grader for explanations, spend expert time validating the grader, and run each candidate in its intended production configuration.
Immediately LLM-grade labels and explanations for all 4,000 to meet the deadline, measuring p95 and cost in production configurations.
