questions.prompt:
A team classifying customer inquiries into six categories with the Claude API must raise accuracy from 78% to 90%. It has 6,000 labeled historical inquiries, about 50 tokens each. Although 90% is the target, all four constraints below are mandatory.

- Category definitions change **every quarter** and must be updated **within one day, without retraining**.
- **Input must not exceed 4,000 tokens** per request because of the monthly cost cap.
- Response **p95 must remain within two seconds**; it is currently 1.7 seconds.
- **No vendor changes or new infrastructure** are permitted.

Initial measurements are:

| Configuration | Accuracy | p95 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Four diverse examples per category: 24 total, about 1,200 tokens | 86% | 1.7 seconds |
| The above configuration with effort increased one level | 88% | All requests take 2.6 seconds |
| Increase effort only for low-confidence requests, about 15% of traffic | About 89% | Only low-confidence requests take 2.6 seconds |

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Include four diverse examples per category inside `<example>` tags and iteratively improve the configuration using a held-out evaluation set.
Place all 6,000 labeled inquiries at the beginning of the prompt; update affected examples and redeploy when definitions change.
Use the example configuration, then reclassify only low-confidence requests, about 15%, with higher effort and evaluate accuracy on a held-out set.
Train a separate classifier on the 6,000 labeled inquiries, serve it on an internal server, and retrain it whenever definitions change.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are [definition changes within one day], [at most 4,000 input tokens], [two-second p95], and [no new infrastructure]. Claude's prompting guidance recommends three to five relevant, diverse examples to avoid learning unintended patterns, separated from instructions with `<example>` tags. Its evaluation guidance recommends measuring changes on a held-out set. Prompt examples can be edited directly when definitions change.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It satisfies all four constraints. The tradeoff is that the measured 86% may fall short of the 90% target; only evaluation can establish whether subsequent improvements reach it.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: The 6,000 inquiries total roughly 300,000 tokens, far above the 4,000-token cap. It uses the most labels but violates the cost constraint.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Its roughly 89% accuracy is highest, but 15% of requests slow down, exceeding 5%, so p95 rises toward 2.6 seconds and breaches the limit. Applying the change to a minority of requests does not preserve p95 when more than the slowest 5% are affected.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: It may make strong use of the data, but requires new infrastructure and retraining after each definition change, also jeopardizing the one-day update requirement.

**References**: [Prompting best practices › Examples](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices) · [Define success criteria and build evaluations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests)

questions.title: Making summary tone consistent in the Gemini API
questions.prompt:
A team generates summaries with the Gemini API. Their content is accurate, but tone varies between requests. The team uses a Gemini 3 model released before 3.6. Its constraints are:

- Improve within **two weeks**, with **no migration to Agent Platform**.
- **Preserve current reasoning quality** for summaries.
- **Minimize additional input tokens** per request.

What should the team try first to make tone and style consistent?

options.text: Include 40 sample summaries in every prompt so the model imitates their tone.
Fine-tune a model on consistently toned summaries in Agent Platform and call that model.
Specify the desired tone and persona once in the system instructions, with only a few representative examples.
Lower temperature below its default to reduce randomness and suppress tone variation.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are [no Agent Platform migration], [preserved reasoning quality], and [minimal input-token increase]. Gemini's prompt-strategy documentation recommends placing behavioral constraints, persona, and output-format requirements in system instructions or at the beginning of the prompt, and warns that too many examples may cause overfitting. It also recommends retaining default sampling settings for Gemini 3 models before 3.6. The Gemini API tuning guide states that tuning is unavailable in the Gemini API and is supported through Agent Platform.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Examples can demonstrate tone, but 40 substantially increase input tokens and introduce the documented overfitting risk.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Tuning is unavailable within the Gemini API, so this requires the prohibited migration.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Explicit tone rules and a few examples satisfy all three constraints. The tradeoff is limited coverage of stylistic variation, which must be evaluated.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Documentation recommends retaining defaults for Gemini 3 models before 3.6; changing them may degrade reasoning.

Also note: Gemini 4 and Gemini 3.6 or later ignore custom temperature, top_p, and top_k values.

**References**: [Prompt design strategies › System instructions and few-shot](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies) · [Fine-tuning with the Gemini API](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/model-tuning)

questions.title: Identifying failures that need context optimization
questions.prompt: A team collected five types of model-response failure. Using the two axes in OpenAI's accuracy-optimization guide—context optimization and LLM optimization—select **two** that should be addressed through **context optimization**.

options.text: Tone varies between polite and stiff from one request to another.
The model answers using an old version of an internal policy revised last month.
JSON key names differ between requests.
The structure of the answer changes each time the same question is asked.
The model does not know the name or specifications of a product launched this quarter.

questions.explanation:
The distinction is [knowledge the model lacks] versus [behavioral consistency]. The guide assigns missing, outdated, or private knowledge to context optimization, the response-accuracy axis. Inconsistent format, tone, or reasoning belongs to LLM optimization, the behavioral-consistency axis.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: Tone consistency is behavioral; improve instructions or examples.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: The current policy is a knowledge gap; provide the relevant document as context.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: Inconsistent output format is a behavioral problem.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: Inconsistent structure requires a behavioral intervention.
- **{{option:E}} (Correct)**: Information released after training must be supplied as context.

**References**: [Optimizing LLM accuracy › LLM optimization context](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/optimizing-llm-accuracy)

questions.title: The first investment for a summarization service with mixed failure causes
questions.prompt:
A customer-support summarization team categorized its failures as follows. Its model and API are fixed.

- 50%: incorrect summaries because the model lacks contract-clause knowledge; the terms are **revised monthly**.
- 20%: violations of summary format or section order.
- 30%: reasoning errors when combining conditions, despite knowing the clauses.

Constraints:

- Demonstrate the effect on **the same evaluation set** within this **two-week sprint**.
- Only **80 labeled examples** are available.
- Response p95 must be **within three seconds**, versus 2.7 seconds currently.
- Monthly model costs cannot readily increase.

What should receive **the first investment** this sprint?

options.text: Upload the terms to a document store and add managed retrieval that inserts only clauses relevant to each query.
Greatly increase the number of correctly formatted summary examples in the prompt.
Set reasoning effort to its maximum to improve multi-condition reasoning.
Expand the labeled dataset to thousands of examples and use supervised fine-tuning to learn both the terms and the format.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [50% knowledge gaps and monthly revisions], [80 labels], [three-second p95 versus 2.7 seconds now], and [two weeks]. The accuracy-optimization guide assigns missing or outdated knowledge to context optimization and inconsistent format or reasoning to LLM optimization. Since the largest group is missing knowledge and the terms change monthly, retrieval that can be refreshed by replacing documents targets the largest group most directly.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It targets the largest group, accommodates revisions through document replacement, and allows before-and-after evaluation. The tradeoffs are retrieval misses as a new failure point and additional latency from the extra call. The team must verify that retrieval fits the 0.3-second p95 headroom.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: It addresses only the 20% format group, leaving the largest group unchanged.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Claude's documentation associates higher effort with more thinking and greater latency, putting the three-second limit at risk from a 2.7-second baseline. It also leaves the 50% knowledge gap unresolved.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Expanding 80 labels to thousands can itself exceed the two-week sprint. Terms embedded through training also require retraining after monthly revisions.

**References**: [Optimizing LLM accuracy › LLM optimization context](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/optimizing-llm-accuracy) · [Prompting best practices › Effort and adaptive thinking](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices)

questions.title: Assessing statements about optimization paths
questions.prompt:
A team is discussing OpenAI's accuracy-optimization guide. Answer Yes if each statement agrees with the guide, otherwise No.

1. Context optimization (RAG) and LLM optimization (tuning) are not mutually exclusive and can be combined depending on the problem.
2. Optimization is described as a straight path from context optimization to LLM optimization.
3. Few-shot examples teach the model by demonstrating the desired style rather than describing it.
4. Automated metrics such as ROUGE or BERTScore, or using a model as a judge, can accelerate evaluation iterations.

items.text: Context optimization (RAG) and LLM optimization (tuning) are not mutually exclusive and can be combined depending on the problem.
Optimization is described as a straight path from context optimization to LLM optimization.
Few-shot examples teach the model by demonstrating the desired style rather than describing it.
Automated metrics such as ROUGE or BERTScore, or using a model as a judge, can accelerate evaluation iterations.

questions.explanation:
The guide describes optimization as an iterative cycle of evaluation, hypothesis, change, and reevaluation. Context optimization supplies information the model lacks, whereas LLM optimization improves behavioral consistency; they are separate levers.

- **1 (Yes)**: The guide describes the methods as additive, not exclusive.
- **2 (No)**: It rejects a simple linear path. Since the axes address different problems, evaluation may lead teams in either direction.
- **3 (Yes)**: Few-shot examples teach the desired style by showing rather than telling.
- **4 (Yes)**: The guide recommends automated metrics such as ROUGE and BERTScore, or model judges, to speed up iteration.

Also note: These statements concern how to choose an approach. OpenAI's deprecation notice already restricts new fine-tuning, so practical availability must be checked separately.

**References**: [Optimizing LLM accuracy › LLM optimization context](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/optimizing-llm-accuracy) · [Model optimization](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/model-optimization)

questions.title: Fixing RAG when retrieved results already contain the answer
questions.prompt: A team operating RAG for internal policies finds that the correct clause often appears among the top five retrieved results, yet the model ignores it or gives a different answer. The service uses the Claude API. Which single change is most appropriate?

options.text: Separate retrieved documents with tags, ask the model to extract relevant quotations first, and then answer based on those quotations.
Increase the number of retrieved results from five to 20 to improve the chance of including the correct clause.
Reindex documents into smaller chunks to use finer retrieval units with less information in each chunk.
Upgrade to a larger embedding model and reindex documents so the correct clause ranks higher more often.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [the correct clause is already retrieved] and [the model ignores or misrepresents it]. OpenAI's accuracy-optimization guide classifies wrong answers despite correct context as generation-stage failures and recommends improving instructions. Claude's long-context guidance recommends placing long documents above the question, separating documents with tags, and quoting relevant passages first to focus on important information.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It addresses generation without changing retrieval.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: It addresses missing results. Adding irrelevant context when the answer is already present may increase noise.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: Chunking affects retrieval quality and requires rebuilding the index; it does not resolve the model ignoring a supplied clause.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: It addresses retrieval failures to find the correct clause. Since retrieval already succeeds, this adds reindexing cost with little expected benefit.

**References**: [Optimizing LLM accuracy › LLM optimization context](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/optimizing-llm-accuracy) · [Prompting best practices › Long-context prompting](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices)

questions.title: Choosing a new optimization path after an OpenAI organization stops using fine-tuning
questions.prompt:
Today is 2026-10-17. An OpenAI organization previously operated a fine-tuned model based on `gpt-4.1-mini`, but its **last inference was on 2026-04-20**, with no fine-tuned-model calls since. It now wants a new fine-tuned model to improve response-format compliance. No retirement has been announced for the current base model it can use for prompting. Requirements:

- The solution must **remain operational beyond 2027**.
- **OpenAI must remain the sole vendor**.
- Launch **within six weeks** and measure improvement on the existing evaluation set.

Which path is most appropriate?

options.text: New jobs can be created before 2027-01-06, so create and train a new fine-tuning job during December.
Add new format instructions to the existing fine-tuned model, keep using it instead of the current base model, and revisit migration in 2027.
Use the current base model without fine-tuning, add examples of correctly formatted responses to its prompt, and compare results on the existing evaluation set.
Train a format-compliant model on another vendor's tuning platform and expose it behind an API gateway.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [last inference on 2026-04-20], [operation beyond 2027], and [OpenAI as sole vendor]. OpenAI's deprecation notice states that from 2026-07-02, organizations without fine-tuned-model inference in the preceding 60 days cannot create new fine-tuning jobs. The last inference was 73 days before July 2, so this organization is already restricted. Fine-tuned models also retire with their base models; GPT-4.1 snapshots are removed on 2027-01-14.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: The 2027-01-06 cutoff applies to existing customers with recent inference. This organization lost creation access earlier.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: The model remains callable now but retires with its base model, failing the long-term operation requirement.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It preserves the vendor and long-term availability constraints without fine-tuning. The tradeoffs are additional example tokens and potentially lower compliance than tuning, which must be checked on the existing evaluation set.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: It can work technically but violates the single-vendor requirement.

**References**: [Deprecations › Self-serve fine-tuning](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/deprecations) · [Model optimization](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/model-optimization)

questions.title: Addressing retrieval failures and inconsistent tone in a Claude legal service
questions.prompt:
A team building legal-document search and summarization with the Claude API encounters two problems: (1) everyday query language differs from legal terminology, so relevant clauses are not retrieved; (2) summary tone varies between requests. Anthropic does not offer its own embedding model; its documentation points to Voyage AI. Constraints:

- Improve both problems within four weeks, measuring **each change separately on the same evaluation set**.
- Begin improving tone **this week**.
- Rebuilding the index with domain-specific embeddings takes **two weeks**.
- The query path has **no remaining p95 latency budget**, so no additional query-time stage is allowed.

Which sequence is most appropriate?

options.text: Release domain-specific embeddings and the tone-prompt improvement together, judging their combined effect with one overall evaluation score.
Release improved tone instructions and examples this week, then defer retrieval until next quarter after observing the prompt change.
Add `rerank-3` to rerank initial retrieval results in the query path, and fix tone in the same release.
Release and evaluate the tone prompt separately this week; then separately evaluate and switch to the reindexed domain-specific embedding index.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are [measure each effect separately], [tone this week], [two-week reindexing], and [no extra query-time stage]. Different causes require different remedies. Terminology-related retrieval failures concern whether embeddings capture the domain. Tone is a behavioral issue addressed by Claude's recommended instructions and diverse examples, typically three to five. Anthropic's embeddings documentation discusses legal-domain models such as `voyage-law-2` and rerankers such as `rerank-3`.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: A combined release prevents attribution and ties the tone improvement to reindexing, missing the start-this-week requirement.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Tone improves quickly, but retrieval is not addressed within four weeks.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Reranking adds a call per query and exceeds the latency budget. Releasing tone changes simultaneously also obscures attribution.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: It evaluates changes sequentially and meets the schedule. The tradeoffs are retrieval improvement arriving at least two weeks after tone improvement and storage for both indexes until the switch.

**References**: [Embeddings › Voyage AI models and rerankers](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/embeddings) · [Prompting best practices › Examples](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices) · [Optimizing LLM accuracy](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/optimizing-llm-accuracy)

questions.title: Reducing violations of complex JSON schemas in the Gemini API
questions.prompt:
A team extracts contract fields into nested JSON using the Gemini API. Although the prompt describes the format, missing required keys and wrong types frequently cause parser errors. Requirements:

- Solve the problem **within the Gemini API**, without migrating to Agent Platform.
- **Structurally reduce schema violations during generation**.
- **Minimize additional latency and code changes**.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Add postprocessing that retries the same request up to three times after parsing failures and returns an error if all attempts fail.
Add five valid JSON response examples and strengthen the prompt's descriptions of required key names and types.
Enable structured output with a response schema, and validate the accuracy of values in the application.
Switch to a larger model that follows complex formatting instructions more reliably, and measure the effect on the same evaluation set.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are [reduce structural errors during generation] and [minimal latency and code changes]. Gemini's prompt-strategy guide says prompts can specify simple JSON, but recommends structured output for complex schemas. The structured-output documentation promises syntactically valid JSON, not accurate values, so application-side value validation is still needed.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: It handles errors afterward; each retry increases latency and cost, violating minimal latency growth.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Examples may help but do not enforce structure. Violations can remain and input-token usage rises.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Adding a request schema reduces structural violations at generation time. The tradeoffs are support for only a subset of JSON Schema and possible rejection of very large or deeply nested schemas, which may need simplification.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Better instruction following does not enforce structure. A model change also requires broader regression evaluation and may increase latency and cost.

**References**: [Prompt design strategies › Structured output](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies) · [Structured output](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/structured-output)

questions.title: Diagnosing a RAG regression in a tuned model and evaluating its successor
questions.prompt:
Today is 2026-10-17. A team operating an OpenAI fine-tuned model based on `gpt-4.1-mini` added retrieval context (RAG), and its score on the same evaluation set fell by four points. This week, it wants to (1) identify the regression **case by case** and (2) test whether RAG helps a **configuration that can operate in 2027**: a successor small base model with no announced retirement. Case-level results for the tuned model **without RAG** were saved from the previous evaluation.

Constraints:
- Only **three evaluation runs** are available this week; a run measures one configuration once.
- Make **one change at a time**.
- **No retraining budget** is available.

Select **two** actions that together satisfy both objectives.

options.text: Run the tuned model once with only RAG added, using the same evaluation set and settings; compare against saved no-RAG results to list regressed cases.
Retrain the tuned model with new examples containing retrieved context, then compare case-level scores with the previous model on the same evaluation set.
Switch to the successor base model and add both RAG and example prompts simultaneously, then score the same evaluation set.
Run the successor small base model once without RAG and once with RAG, using the same evaluation set and settings, and compare case-level differences.
Run fresh with-RAG and without-RAG evaluations on both models, ignoring saved results, and compare all four configurations case by case.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are [case-level diagnosis], [operation in 2027], [three runs], [one change at a time], and [no retraining budget]. OpenAI's accuracy guide describes a tuned GPT-4 model scoring 87 BLEU and losing four points after adding RAG: additional context may become noise once the model has learned the behavior. OpenAI's deprecation notice removes the `gpt-4.1-mini` snapshot and derived fine-tuned models on 2027-01-14. Therefore, regression diagnosis requires the current tuned model, whereas the future-configuration test requires the successor. {{option:A}} uses one run and {{option:D}} uses two, totaling three.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Isolating RAG identifies regressed cases. Reusing stored results limits this to one run. The tradeoff is spending a run on a model nearing removal.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Although retraining aligns with the guide's direction, there is no budget. The retrained model would also retire with its base on 2027-01-14, failing the 2027 requirement.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Three simultaneous changes violate the one-change rule and prevent attribution.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: It isolates RAG's effect in the 2027 configuration. Its two runs, plus {{option:A}}, consume the entire allowance. Results from the successor do not explain the tuned model's regression.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: It addresses both goals but wastes saved results and requires four runs instead of three.

**References**: [Optimizing LLM accuracy › LLM optimization context](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/optimizing-llm-accuracy) · [Deprecations › Self-serve fine-tuning](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/deprecations)

questions.title: Designing few-shot examples for Gemini API classification
questions.prompt: You are designing a Gemini API prompt to classify inquiries into eight categories. A fixed parser expects a single category name. The input budget is **1,500 tokens** per request; instructions and format descriptions consume 300 tokens, and each example is about 60 tokens. Select **two** configurations consistent with Gemini's prompting guidance.

options.text: Vary the format across examples so the model does not become tied to one format; include two per category, 16 total.
Use identical tags, spacing, line breaks, and delimiters in every example, and choose the number through evaluation within the token budget.
Choose diverse examples, including boundary cases, for each category, using 16 total to narrow the model's focus.
Use five consistently formatted examples per category, 40 total, to maximize accuracy.
Choose only easy, typical cases, with identical counts and lengths across categories.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are [fixed parser] and [1,500-token budget]. Gemini's prompting guidance recommends including few-shot examples, experimentally determining the right number, and avoiding excessive examples that may cause overfitting. Structure and formatting—tags, spaces, line breaks, and delimiters—should remain consistent, while diverse examples narrow the model's focus. The budget permits at most (1,500 − 300) ÷ 60 = 20 examples.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Sixteen examples fit at about 1,260 tokens, but mixed formatting may destabilize output and break the fixed parser. The guide recommends consistency.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Consistent formatting and experimental selection of example count satisfy the parser and budget constraints.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Diverse cases narrow the task, and 16 fit within the budget.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Formatting is consistent, but 40 examples total about 2,700 tokens, exceeding the budget and introducing overfitting risk.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: It can fit the budget, but easy cases omit boundaries and fail to provide the recommended diversity.

**References**: [Prompt design strategies › Few-shot examples](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies)

questions.title: Multi-step reasoning errors despite correct knowledge and formatting
questions.prompt:
A Claude API service calculates and explains billing conditions. Most errors occur when several conditions must be combined sequentially. Analysis shows that the prompt already includes the necessary policy knowledge and output formatting is correct. Constraints:

- **No additional query-time calls** are permitted.
- Any monthly model-cost increase must remain within **the current per-token pricing structure**; changing model tiers is prohibited.
- Apply the change within one day and evaluate it on the same test set.

Which change is most appropriate?

options.text: Upgrade one model tier to improve reasoning with the same prompt and compare evaluation results.
Create five additional worked examples showing calculations step by step and include them in every prompt.
Add query-time policy retrieval so only relevant billing clauses enter context.
Keep adaptive thinking, increase effort by one level, and measure both quality and latency on the same evaluation set.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [sufficient knowledge and correct format], [no extra calls], and [no model-tier change]. Claude's prompting guidance states that models from 4.6 onward use adaptive thinking; reasoning depth depends on effort and query complexity, with higher effort allowing more thinking. Increasing effort is a direct first adjustment for reasoning failures.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Reasoning may improve, but changing tiers is prohibited and may substantially raise per-token prices.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: The issue is reasoning depth rather than format, so the effect may be limited while every request gains input tokens.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Knowledge is already present, and an extra retrieval call violates the call-count constraint.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: It addresses reasoning depth without another call or a different model. The tradeoffs are potentially more output tokens and higher latency, both of which must be measured.

**References**: [Prompting best practices › Effort and adaptive thinking](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices)

questions.title: Writing success criteria before changing a prompt
questions.prompt: A team building a sentiment classifier with the Claude API is documenting success criteria before changing its prompt. Baseline F1 is 0.78, and the best preliminary prompt experiment reached 0.86. Which statement best matches Anthropic's criteria of specificity, measurability, achievability, and relevance?

options.text: The classifier improves F1 above the current 0.78 baseline on 10,000 diverse held-out posts.
The classifier achieves F1 of at least 0.85 on 10,000 diverse held-out posts, improving on the baseline.
The classifier achieves F1 of at least 0.95 on 200 posts handpicked by the development team.
The classifier maintains p95 response latency of at most 200 ms per post.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [document criteria before prompt changes] and [baseline F1 0.78, preliminary best 0.86]. Anthropic's evaluation guidance says success criteria should be specific, measurable through metrics such as F1 or accuracy, achievable based on benchmarks and preliminary experiments, and relevant to the goal. It gives the example of F1 of at least 0.85 on 10,000 diverse held-out posts.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: It is measurable but lacks a specific required improvement. Even 0.01 could count as success.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It specifies a metric, threshold, evaluation size, and improvement over baseline. The target is below the observed 0.86 maximum and therefore achievable.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: It is measurable, but 0.95 is far above preliminary performance. Two hundred developer-selected posts also fail to represent diverse real-world traffic.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: It is specific and measurable but addresses latency rather than classification quality. Latency should be a separate criterion.

**References**: [Define success criteria and build evaluations › Define your success criteria](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests)

questions.title: A Gemini chatbot that gets yesterday's news and current exchange rates wrong
questions.prompt:
A Gemini API customer-support chatbot answers questions about yesterday's news and today's exchange rates incorrectly. The team asks whether fine-tuning can fix this. Constraints:

- **No migration to Agent Platform**.
- Future news topics and numerical queries are **unpredictable**, and there are **no operations staff** for separate data collection and updates.
- Answers must **show sources**.

Which remedy is most appropriate?

options.text: Create a question-answer dataset of yesterday's news and exchange rates, fine-tune on it, and retrain daily with new data.
Add today's date to the system instructions so the model recognizes that current information is needed.
Regularly collect news and exchange rates and append them to the system instructions for every request.
Enable grounding with Google Search and display sources using the response's URL citation metadata.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are [unpredictable current-information questions], [no operations staff], [source attribution], and [no migration]. Gemini's prompt-strategy guide recommends Google Search grounding when current information is needed. The grounding documentation says the model decides when to search and returns URL citation metadata linking text spans to sources. The Gemini API tuning guide states that tuning is unavailable in that API.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: It requires migration and ongoing labor. Fine-tuning is not an appropriate way to track facts that change daily.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Supplying the date does not give the model facts it does not know.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: It covers collected topics only; unpredictable questions outside that coverage remain unanswered. Collection and updating also require staff.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: It satisfies the requirements. The tradeoffs are search-related request costs—for Gemini 3 and later, based on executed search queries—and dependence on search-result quality.

**References**: [Prompt design strategies › Grounding](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies) · [Grounding with Google Search](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/google-search) · [Fine-tuning with the Gemini API](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/model-tuning)

questions.title: Prerequisites before deciding on fine-tuning
questions.prompt: A team is considering supervised fine-tuning to improve response-format compliance. Following the process assumed by OpenAI's model-optimization documentation, select **two** things to establish **before starting a tuning job** as evidence for deciding whether tuning is needed.

options.text: Create a fixed evaluation set and measure the current prompt's baseline score.
Label production logs and prepare them as candidate training data.
Optimize the prompt as far as possible, then categorize the remaining failures.
Build the serving environment and deployment pipeline for the tuned model.
Switch to the smallest base model and calculate the projected cost difference after tuning.

questions.explanation:
The key phrase is [before starting tuning]. OpenAI's model-optimization process establishes an evaluation baseline, prompts the model with context and instructions, and only optionally fine-tunes if performance remains insufficient. Its accuracy guide likewise starts with prompt engineering and an evaluation set before heavier interventions.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: A baseline enables comparison with the tuned model on the same evaluation set.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: Preparing training material follows the decision to tune. It does not supply the baseline or remaining failure categories needed to justify that decision.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It eliminates problems that prompting can solve and checks whether the remaining failures concern behavior.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: overengineering)**: This is needed after deciding to tune, not as a prerequisite for that decision.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: This concerns cost optimization, and changing models also changes the baseline.

questions.title: Choosing a cost-reduction path instead of distillation
questions.prompt:
Today is 2026-10-17. An OpenAI team planned to reduce costs by distilling a large model's responses into a fine-tuned `gpt-4.1-mini`, but learned about the fine-tuning retirement schedule. The team is an existing customer with fine-tuned-model inference within the last 60 days, so it can still create jobs in December. Requirements:

- Reduce per-request cost by **at least 40%** from the current large model's $0.0100.

- **Operate beyond 2027** and retain **OpenAI as sole vendor**.
- Thousands of large-model responses that pass evaluation criteria are already available.

Initial measurements follow. The successor small model is an OpenAI base model with no announced retirement.

| Configuration | Cost per request | Accuracy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Keep large model; compress prompts and cache | $0.0085 | 96.0% |
| Successor small model; three passing responses as examples | $0.0046 | 94.8% |
| Successor small model; 20 passing responses as examples | $0.0071 | 96.0% |
| Distillation-tuned `gpt-4.1-mini` | $0.0035 | 96.2% |
| Another vendor's small model; three passing examples | $0.0042 | 95.0% |

Which path is most appropriate?

options.text: Use three passing responses as examples with the successor small model and measure accuracy and cost on the same evaluation set.
Use 20 passing responses as examples with the successor small model and measure accuracy and cost on the same evaluation set.
Keep the large model, compress the prompt, and apply caching.
Proceed with `gpt-4.1-mini` distillation, finish training in December, and evaluate accuracy on the same set.
Migrate to another vendor's small model with three passing responses as examples and evaluate it on the same set.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are [at least 40% savings], [at most 1.5 percentage points lost], [operation beyond 2027], and [OpenAI only]. OpenAI's distillation process first optimizes the large model's prompt against evaluation criteria, builds a dataset from passing responses, and tunes a smaller model. However, `gpt-4.1-mini` and derived tuned models are removed on 2027-01-14. The targets are cost at most $0.0060 and accuracy at least 94.5%. Passing responses from the first distillation stage can instead serve as prompt examples for the successor without tuning.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: $0.0046 is a 54% reduction, and 94.8% is a 1.2-point loss, satisfying both targets and operational constraints. The tradeoff is accuracy 1.4 points below tuning and close to the allowed loss, requiring reevaluation on the same set.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Accuracy remains 96.0%, but $0.0071 saves only 29%, below 40%, because extra examples increase input tokens.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Continuity, vendor, and accuracy requirements are met, but savings are only 15%.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: It follows the documented distillation method and has excellent cost and accuracy, but the resulting model is removed on 2027-01-14.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Cost and accuracy fit, but the single-vendor requirement does not.

questions.title: Embedding a 20,000-token contract as one vector

A legal team building Claude-based contract search indexes contracts using Voyage AI models recommended in Anthropic documentation. Each contract is about 20,000 tokens; a vector-database row limit requires **one vector per contract**. Conditions:

- **At most 512 dimensions** because of database costs.
- Input **the entire contract at once** for contract-level retrieval.
- Maximize legal-search accuracy; batch indexing allows flexibility on latency and unit cost.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Split each contract into two segments of at most 16,000 tokens, embed them with `voyage-law-2`, and average the two into one 1,024-dimensional vector.

- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Supports 512 dimensions and document context, but creates multiple chunk vectors per contract.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Meets the hard constraints but optimizes latency/cost rather than accuracy when those budgets have headroom.

questions.title: Fixing vector-store search for verbose conversational queries
questions.prompt:
A team uploads support documents to an OpenAI vector store and directly calls the retrieval `search` API for RAG. Verbose customer questions such as "Hello, the product I bought last week suddenly won't turn on—what should I do?" retrieve irrelevant documents. A cleaned query such as "fix power not turning on" works. Conditions:

- **Do not degrade current retrieval quality** for already-clean standalone questions.
- **Do not increase retrieved-result tokens** sent to the model.
- Change **search-call settings only, without adding application code**.
- Added retrieval-stage p95 latency must be **at most 150 ms**; one additional retrieval-stage LLM call has been measured at about 120 ms.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Increase `ranking_options.score_threshold` to filter low-relevance chunks from results.
Enable `rewrite_query` and log the returned `search_query` field to inspect the actual query used.
Increase `max_num_results` from its default of 10 to 50 to increase the chance of including the correct chunk.
Add a rule-based preprocessing function that removes greetings and filler before search calls.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [settings only, no added code] and [preserve clean-query quality]. OpenAI retrieval documentation says enabling `rewrite_query` automatically rewrites a query for better retrieval and returns the rewritten text in `search_query`. It converts verbose conversational wording into search-friendly form while largely preserving already-clean questions, requiring one setting.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: The documentation notes that higher thresholds retain more relevant chunks but may discard useful ones, reducing results even for currently successful standalone questions.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Meets the three conditions and latency limit (about 120 ms added versus 150 ms allowed). It nearly consumes latency headroom, and rewriting can change meaning, so inspect `search_query` and validate on an evaluation set.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: More results increase tokens while leaving the underlying reason the correct chunk ranks poorly unchanged.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: May help but requires creating and maintaining preprocessing code, violating settings-only changes. Unhandled expressions remain problematic.

Also note: The documentation describes `rewrite_query` as a `search` option; do not assume it is enabled by default.

**References**: [Retrieval](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/retrieval) · [File search](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-file-search)

questions.title: Fitting 80 million vectors into memory while preserving recall
questions.prompt:
A retrieval team serves an ANN index of 80 million 1,024-dimensional float32 vectors. Raw vectors alone occupy about 328 GB; only **100 GB** is available for vectors. Conditions and measurements:

- Maintain **recall@10 of at least 0.95** on actual query samples.
- **p95 latency at most 120 ms**, currently 85 ms.
- **No document re-embedding calls**. The model supports truncating leading dimensions without a new call.
- **No budget for additional memory nodes**.
- Measurements: int8 quantization alone gives recall@10 0.94; one-bit binary quantization alone gives 0.88; truncating to 512 dimensions and renormalizing gives 0.96. Rescoring the compressed index's top 100 candidates using original float32 vectors on SSD raises recall@10 by about 0.03 and p95 by about 25 ms.

Choose **two index changes to combine** to satisfy all conditions.

options.text: Use one-bit binary quantization and return candidate rankings without rescoring.
Use int8 scalar quantization for vectors loaded into the index.
Truncate stored vectors to the first 512 dimensions, renormalize, and index them directly as float32.
Keep original float32 vectors on SSD and rescore only the top 100 candidates with them.
Keep original float32 vectors unchanged and shard them across four memory nodes.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [about 100 GB], [recall@10 at least 0.95], and [no additional-node budget]. Int8 quantization reduces vector size to roughly one quarter (82 GB), fitting memory, but alone reaches only 0.94 recall. Retrieving a broad candidate set from the compressed index and rescoring with original SSD float32 vectors corrects rankings and restores recall. Using the measured 0.03 gain gives approximately 0.97 recall; p95 becomes about 85 + 25 = 110 ms. Azure AI Search documentation likewise describes quarter-size int8 quantization and rescoring oversampled candidates with original full-precision vectors to offset compression loss. The recall/latency values in this question are hypothetical prior measurements.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: About 10 GB fits, but measured recall of 0.88 misses 0.95.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Compresses enough to fit memory. Alone it misses recall, so pair it with {{option:D}}.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Recall 0.96 is adequate, but 512-dimensional float32 requires about 164 GB, exceeding memory.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Corrects compressed-index ranking with originals to meet recall. It requires separate original-vector storage and raises p95 to about 110 ms, leaving only 10 ms headroom; confirm under load.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Preserves recall and latency but needs four nodes, violating the expansion-budget constraint.

**References**: [Azure AI Search › Vector quantization and rescoring](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/vector-search-how-to-quantization) · [Gemini API Embeddings › output\_dimensionality and normalization](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/embeddings)

questions.title: Query and document formats when moving a QA chatbot to gemini-embedding-2
questions.prompt:
An internal FAQ chatbot is migrating from `gemini-embedding-001` to `gemini-embedding-2`. Existing code sets `task_type=QUESTION_ANSWERING` for queries and `task_type=RETRIEVAL_DOCUMENT` for documents. The new model does not accept `task_type`, so instructions must be written into input text. Conditions:

- Retrieval is for **answering questions**.
- Use **different, asymmetric formats** for queries and documents.
- Use **one consistent document format for every indexed document**. FAQ documents have no titles.

Which input format is most appropriate?

Embed queries as `task: search result | query: {content}` and documents as `title: none | text: {content}`.
Embed queries as `task: question answering | query: {content}` and documents as plain body text without a prefix.
Embed queries as `task: question answering | query: {content}` and documents as `title: none | text: {content}`.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [asymmetric formats] and [retrieval for question answering]. Gemini embeddings documentation says `gemini-embedding-2` accepts task instructions in input text rather than `task_type`. For QA retrieval, use `task: question answering | query: {content}` for queries and `title: {title} | text: {content}` for documents. Use `title: none` when no title exists and apply the respective query/document formats consistently.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Uses a symmetric approach suited to classification/clustering, violating asymmetric retrieval. Calls succeed, but document formatting is wrong.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: The document format is correct, but the query prefix is for general search rather than question answering.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Query formatting is correct, but documents lack the required consistent document format.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Meets all three conditions. Every indexed document must be re-embedded in this format; old-model vectors cannot be reused.

questions.title: Indexing three-minute training videos with gemini-embedding-2
questions.prompt:
A team will index 400 three-minute (180-second) MP4 training videos with Gemini API's `gemini-embedding-2`. Audio is already indexed separately as transcripts. Requirements:

- When users describe a scene, return **the matching segment's start time**.
- Make **the entire video** searchable.
- **Do not miss scenes crossing segment boundaries**.

Place the split segments directly as multiple parts in one request's `contents` and call once.
Embed only the first 120 seconds and leave the rest unindexed.
Cut into exactly 120-second segments without overlap and embed each separately.

Gemini embeddings documentation limits video input to 120 seconds, uniformly samples long videos into 32 frames, and does not process video-file audio tracks. It recommends overlapping segments for longer videos. Multiple parts placed directly in `contents` produce one aggregated embedding; wrapping each input in a separate `Content` produces separate embeddings.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: The recommended approach respects the 120-second limit while retaining boundary scenes.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Separate segment vectors allow returning the matching start time. More vectors—at least two per video—increase storage and call costs.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: One aggregated vector cannot identify a segment start time.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Respects the input limit but fails full-video coverage.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Produces segment vectors but splits boundary scenes without overlap, contrary to the recommendation.

Also note: Audio-track omission is not a problem here because transcripts are already indexed. Do not expect video vectors to retrieve spoken dialogue.

questions.title: Assessing domain-adaptive embedding tuning
questions.prompt:
A legal-document retrieval team will tune a general embedding model for its domain. It has 3,000 query/correct-document pairs, allocating 2,000 to tuning and 1,000 to evaluation. Current recall@10 is 0.78. Mark statements Yes if consistent with general embedding-training and retrieval-evaluation principles, otherwise No.

1. To distinguish similar clauses differing only by clause number, include similar but incorrect documents (hard negatives) in training rather than only randomly sampled incorrect documents.
2. A recall@10 increase from 0.78 to 0.80 measured on 1,000 pairs can be interpreted with the same confidence whether evaluation has 1,000 or 100 pairs.
3. Compare pre/post-tuning recall@k on the 1,000 held-out pairs using the same corpus and the same k.
4. Automatically mined hard negatives can contain actually correct documents (false negatives), so human review of a sample is advisable.

items.text: To distinguish similar clauses differing only by clause number, include similar but incorrect documents (hard negatives) in training rather than only randomly sampled incorrect documents.
A recall@10 increase from 0.78 to 0.80 measured on 1,000 pairs can be interpreted with the same confidence whether evaluation has 1,000 or 100 pairs.
Compare pre/post-tuning recall@k on the 1,000 held-out pairs using the same corpus and the same k.
Automatically mined hard negatives can contain actually correct documents (false negatives), so human review of a sample is advisable.

questions.explanation:
Embedding training learns what to place close together or far apart from the composition of positive pairs and negatives. Evaluation must compare under identical conditions using data excluded from training. This question tests general ML principles.

- **1 (Yes)**: Random negatives are often too easy to teach fine distinctions; hard negatives directly provide that signal.
- **2 (No)**: Smaller evaluation sets increase recall-estimation uncertainty, so the same 0.02 difference may be chance. Consider both pair count and uncertainty when judging improvement.
- **3 (Yes)**: Evaluating training pairs inflates scores. Use held-out data under consistent conditions. OpenAI's supervised-fine-tuning guidance also recommends separating a holdout from the same dataset before training.
- **4 (Yes)**: Similar documents can actually be correct; labeling them negative pushes away valid signals. Sample review reduces this risk.

**References**: [Supervised fine-tuning](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/supervised-fine-tuning)

questions.title: Allocating batch and synchronous calls for three million reindexed chunks
questions.prompt:
A search team will re-embed and index three million document chunks using OpenAI embeddings. Query embeddings continue through synchronous `/v1/embeddings` in the same project. Conditions:

- **50,000 new-policy chunks (about 20 million tokens) must be searchable within 12 hours**.
- Embedding the remaining **2.95 million must cost half the synchronous rate**.
- Synchronous capacity remaining after query-service traffic is **about 40,000 tokens/minute**, which must not be exceeded.

Which execution plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Submit all three million through Batch API as 60 batches of at most 50,000 inputs, staying within queued-token limits.
Send all three million synchronously to `/v1/embeddings`, increasing concurrency when query traffic is low.
Rate-limit synchronous calls for the urgent 50,000 to available headroom; submit the remaining 2.95 million through Batch API as 59 batches of at most 50,000 inputs.
Increase synchronous concurrency to finish the urgent 50,000 in one hour; submit the other 2.95 million as 59 Batch API batches of at most 50,000 inputs.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [50,000 within 12 hours], [half-price remaining 2.95 million], and [40,000 tokens/minute headroom]. OpenAI Batch API offers a 50% discount, with only a `24h` completion window; saying it usually finishes sooner is not a shorter deadline guarantee. Embedding batches allow at most 50,000 inputs each. Batch limits are separate from per-model synchronous limits, so batches do not consume those synchronous tokens. Batch creation is limited to 2,000 per hour.

| Plan | Urgent 50,000 | Remaining 2.95 million | Violation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| {{option:A}} | Batch, 24-hour window with no 12-hour guarantee | Included in 60 total batches | 12-hour deadline |
| {{option:B}} | Synchronous | Synchronous | Half-price requirement and headroom |
| {{option:C}} | Synchronous at 40,000 tokens/minute: about 500 minutes, or 8.3 hours | 59 batches | None |
| {{option:D}} | Synchronous in one hour: about 330,000 tokens/minute | 59 batches | Headroom |

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Lowest cost, but a 24-hour window cannot guarantee the urgent items within 12 hours.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Can meet timing but charges full price for 2.95 million chunks and risks exceeding capacity needed by query traffic.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Meets all three conditions. Urgent embeddings pay full price; operations must maintain both a throttled synchronous path for over eight hours and a batch path. Only about 3.7 hours remain before the deadline, making long retries risky.

questions.title: Embedding migration and video-indexing plan
questions.prompt: Which migration plan best meets [Requirements 1 and 2]? Assume the final goal includes visual-description search and retains the existing self-managed vector database.
questions.context:

options.text: Build a new index alongside the old one. Re-embed FAQs in batches, split videos into overlapping segments of at most 120 seconds and embed each separately, then switch queries after validation.

Add only new material to the existing index. Generate PDF and overlapping video-segment vectors with `gemini-embedding-2` beside existing FAQ vectors, and search everything using queries embedded only by `gemini-embedding-2`.
Build a parallel new index, re-embed FAQs in batches, index only video transcripts as text embeddings, then switch queries after validation.
Build a parallel new index, immediately re-embed FAQs through real-time calls, index overlapping video segments of at most 120 seconds separately, then switch queries after validation.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are visual-description segment retrieval in [Requirement 1], and uninterrupted operation plus batch-price budgeting in [Requirement 2]. Gemini documentation says the embedding spaces of `gemini-embedding-001` and `gemini-embedding-2` are incompatible, requiring re-embedding all data. Videos are limited to 120 seconds, audio tracks are not processed, and longer videos should be split with overlap. Gemini Batch API supports embeddings at 50% of standard rates, with a 24-hour target turnaround. A parallel new index preserves old-index service until validation finishes.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Handles incompatible spaces, video limits, batch budgeting, and continuity. Both indexes incur storage costs until switching; the 24-hour batch target requires more than a day's slack, and segmentation increases vector count.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Avoids interruption but compares old `001` FAQ vectors with new `2` query vectors across incompatible spaces.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Meets cost/continuity needs, but transcripts alone cannot retrieve visual charts or board writing. It can serve phase one, not the final goal.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: The structure is right, but real-time re-embedding forgoes the 50% batch discount and exceeds the budget basis. More than a day's slack permits batching.

Also note: The developer's assumption about embedded video dialogue contradicts documentation. Video audio tracks are not processed; spoken-content search requires transcripts.

questions.title: Choosing Agent Platform tuning for 5,000 single-label examples
questions.prompt:
A team with Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform tuning access classifies customer inquiries into 12 categories. It has 5,000 inquiries, each with one correct category, and accuracy has plateaued despite prompt refinement. Conditions:

- **No staff** to design and validate a reward function.
- **No additional data creation**, including preference pairs.
- **No increase in per-request input tokens**.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Use the 5,000 inquiry/correct-category examples for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of a classifier.
Design a new reward function scoring correct-label matches and perform reinforcement-learning (RL) tuning.
Create 5,000 new preference pairs of correct versus incorrect categories and perform preference tuning.
Include all 5,000 examples in the prompt of every request.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [single correct-category labels], [no reward-function staff], and [no new data]. Agent Platform describes supervised tuning as adapting behavior for classification, summarization, and chat using labeled datasets; reinforcement tuning uses user-defined reward functions. Input/single-answer pairs directly fit SFT. Preference tuning compares chosen and rejected responses, also reflected in OpenAI's DPO data structure.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Uses existing data without extra staffing or input tokens. Category-definition changes require retuning, and this tuning environment is Agent Platform.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Can work, but requires unavailable reward-function design/validation staff.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Requires constructing new pairs, violating the no-new-data constraint.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Avoids tuning but greatly increases input tokens on every request.

Also note: Check model-specific documentation for data formats and hyperparameters. This question concerns method selection only.

**References**: [Supervised fine-tuning (Agent Platform)](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/models/tuning/supervised-tuning) · [Reinforcement tuning (Agent Platform)](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/models/tuning/reinforcement-tuning) · [Direct preference optimization (OpenAI)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/direct-preference-optimization)

questions.title: Aligning response tone with 4,000 staff preference pairs
questions.prompt:
A team operating tuning on Agent Platform is improving support-response tone. It has 4,000 pairs in which support staff selected the better of two responses to the same inquiry; the goal is to avoid the rejected response's tone. The team already operates tuning on Agent Platform. Conditions:

- Train on **both chosen and rejected signals**.
- **Do not build a new reward function or reward model**.
- **Do not lengthen system instructions**.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Use only the 4,000 chosen responses as SFT data to learn tone.
Build a reward model from the preference pairs and use its scores for RL tuning.
Use the 4,000 chosen/rejected response pairs directly for preference tuning.
Place five representative chosen responses in system instructions as tone examples.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [use both signals] and [no new reward model]. Agent Platform provides preference tuning separately from supervised and reinforcement tuning; reinforcement tuning uses user-defined reward functions. Chosen/rejected pairs are the general preference-optimization structure, also used by OpenAI DPO.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Discards the rejected-response signal, failing to use both.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Uses both signals but requires building and validating a new reward model.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Uses both signals without additional construction. Inconsistent staff preferences can weaken learning, so assess agreement rates.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Avoids tuning but lengthens system instructions and ignores rejection signals.

Also note: Check the relevant documentation for preference-data formats and supported models. This question concerns method selection only.

**References**: [Preference tuning (Agent Platform)](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/models/tuning/preference-tuning/use) · [Reinforcement tuning (Agent Platform)](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/models/tuning/reinforcement-tuning) · [Direct preference optimization (OpenAI)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/direct-preference-optimization)

questions.title: Tuning defect-report classification with site photos
questions.prompt:
An equipment company classifies defect reports containing JPEG site photos and short descriptions into 12 types. It has 6,000 reports labeled with the correct type and can tune on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. Its supervised-tuning documentation has modality-specific guides for text, documents, images, audio, video, and function calls. Conditions:

- Give photos **directly as image inputs**, without a preceding image-to-text stage.
- **No staff to build a reward function**.
- Photo information **must actually inform classification**.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Use another model to caption photos into text, then perform text-input SFT.
Perform image-input supervised tuning using photos, report descriptions, and correct-type labels.
Extract only description text for text SFT and exclude photos from training.
Use photos and descriptions but design a new correct-answer reward function for reinforcement tuning.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [direct image input] and [actual use of visual information]. Agent Platform supervised-tuning documentation includes an image-input guide. SFT adapts classification behavior using labeled data, matching the available input/correct-type examples.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Can work but adds an image-to-text stage, violating direct input; visual details missed by captions are lost to classification.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Directly uses images and existing labels. Check the modality documentation for supported models, image counts, sizes, and other limits.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Text-only descriptions leave photo information unused, violating the last condition.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: RL requires a user-defined reward function that the team lacks staff to build.

Also note: Image support varies by model; confirm supported tuning modalities before starting.

**References**: [Supervised fine-tuning (Agent Platform)](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/models/tuning/supervised-tuning) · [Reinforcement tuning (Agent Platform)](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/models/tuning/reinforcement-tuning)

questions.title: Why tuning fails with a Gemini Developer API key
questions.prompt: A developer calls `client.tunings.tune(...)` from a Python client created with a Gemini Developer API key (`genai.Client(api_key=...)`), and it fails. The training-data format and model name match the tuning documentation examples. Which action addresses the cause?

Retry using an older 1.5 Flash model name that previously supported tuning.
Issue a new API key in AI Studio and retry the same call.
Create an Agent Platform client using project/region authentication and invoke tuning in that environment.

Gemini API tuning documentation says no models currently support tuning in Gemini API or AI Studio; tuning is supported on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. Google Gen AI Python SDK documentation also limits `client.tunings.tune` to Agent Platform. The cause is execution environment, not call format.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: File upload does not address this failure's cause.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: After the tuning-capable 1.5 Flash model was discontinued, no tunable Gemini API model remained.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: Reissuing a key addresses authentication errors, not environment restrictions.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Moves to an environment supporting tuning.

Also note: Gemini API documentation states there are no immediate plans to bring tuning support to Gemini API.
