questions.title: Adjusting DPO beta to preserve more original behavior
questions.prompt: In an ongoing DPO experiment, an existing OpenAI customer finds that adapting to preference data has substantially changed the model's original general behavior. The next experiment should **preserve more original behavior**. Current `beta` is 0.1. (Existing customers also cannot create new fine-tuning jobs from January 6, 2027; this question tests understanding of the method.) Which adjustment is most appropriate?

options.text: Lower `beta` from 0.1 to 0.01.
Raise `beta` from 0.1 to 1.0.
Keep `beta` unchanged and rewrite `preferred_output` responses to be longer.
Set `beta` to `auto` and let the platform choose.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clue is [preserve more original behavior]. OpenAI DPO documentation defines `beta` from 0 to 2: higher values produce more conservative learning that preserves prior behavior; lower values follow new preferences more aggressively. The default `auto` uses a platform-chosen value.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Moves in the opposite direction; lower beta follows new preferences more aggressively.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Higher beta conservatively preserves original behavior. It may reduce tone/style gains from preferences, so measure both effects on the same evaluation set.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: Changing response length addresses data quality; beta controls deviation from prior behavior.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Documentation does not guarantee that the automatic value preserves more prior behavior.

Also note: DPO currently supports text input/output only and trains on single-turn conversations.

**References**: [Direct preference optimization](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/direct-preference-optimization) · [Deprecations › Update to OpenAI's self-serve fine-tuning](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/deprecations)

questions.title: Training only selected assistant messages in multi-turn SFT
questions.prompt:
One line of an OpenAI SFT training file contains user questions followed by three assistant responses: (1) factual product specifications, (2) an empathetic response, and (3) a closing greeting. The team wants to exclude (1) from training and train only on (2) and (3). Conditions:

- Keep (1) **as context for later responses**.
- Preserve **one conversation per line**.

(Even existing customers cannot create new tuning jobs from January 6, 2027; this question tests data-format understanding.) Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Delete message (1) from the conversation and train on the remaining two responses.
Change message (1)'s `role` to `user`, retaining it as context like a user utterance.
Set `"weight": 0` on message (1) and `"weight": 1` on messages (2) and (3).
Split into three lines, repeating context for each assistant response, then remove the line for (1).

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [(1) remains context] and [one conversation per line]. OpenAI fine-tuning best practices allow multiple user/assistant messages per line for multi-turn conversations. Assign `"weight": 0` to assistant messages excluded from training and `"weight": 1` to those included.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Deletion removes specification context assumed by response (2).
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Retains context but changes conversational structure from actual inference. Documentation recommends matching training examples to inference format.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Selects training targets while preserving context and structure. Validate that message-level weights are not omitted when preparing files.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Adds lines and repeated-context tokens, violating one conversation per line.

Also note: Keep examples within documented token limits and validate format before uploading.

**References**: [Fine-tuning best practices](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/fine-tuning-best-practices) · [Deprecations › Update to OpenAI's self-serve fine-tuning](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/deprecations)

questions.title: RFT training reward rises while validation reward stalls
questions.prompt: An existing OpenAI customer running reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) sees `train_reward_mean` steadily rising while `valid_reward_mean` stalls. Training is still running. (Even existing customers cannot create new tuning jobs from January 6, 2027; this question tests diagnosis.) Choose **two appropriate diagnostic or response actions**.

options.text: Increase epochs and train longer with the same settings.
Select the checkpoint with the highest `train_reward_mean` as the final model.
Read outputs on representative prompts to look for patterns that fool the grader into awarding high scores.
Switch to a smaller model grader to reduce grading-call costs and continue training unchanged.
Pause the job to create a checkpoint, evaluate on a held-out test set, then decide whether to resume.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clue is [rising training reward, flat validation reward]. OpenAI RFT guidance warns about overfitting and reward hacking, where incorrect answers receive high grader scores; inspect behavior on representative prompts before deployment. `train_reward_mean` varies substantially because step data differs, making cross-step comparison difficult, whereas `valid_reward_mean` is more stable. The documented response is to pause, create a checkpoint, evaluate on a held-out test set, and then resume as appropriate; poor results call for fixing training data or the grader before rerunning.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Longer training with flat validation may deepen overfitting/reward hacking and spends without diagnosis.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Training reward is noisy across steps; retained checkpoints are the top three by `valid_reward_mean`.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Directly checks for reward hacking as recommended.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Cuts cost but changes grading reliability, making reward-hacking diagnosis harder.
- **{{option:E}} (Correct)**: Follows pause/evaluate/resume guidance, at the cost of evaluation time and interruption.

Also note: Graders should be reliable and difficult to exploit. If lucky answers can earn high rewards, the learning signal weakens and the task should be redesigned.

**References**: [Reinforcement fine-tuning](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reinforcement-fine-tuning) · [Deprecations › Update to OpenAI's self-serve fine-tuning](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/deprecations)

questions.title: Reusing 3,000 labels without Claude tuning
questions.prompt:
A Claude API inquiry-classification team has 3,000 inquiry/correct-category labels collected for supervised learning last quarter. It has decided not to tune and wants to reuse them for accuracy evaluation. This quarter, the boundary between "refund" and "exchange" changed; about 700 old labels fall in those categories. Conditions:

- Report scores reflecting the new definitions **this week**.
- Labelers can relabel **400 examples this week**.
- The four **unchanged categories must remain directly comparable** with last quarter's scores.
- **No new infrastructure or external contracts**.

Which use is most appropriate?

options.text: Plan to relabel all 3,000 under the new definitions, starting with 400 this week, and postpone scores until completion.
Relabel 400 of the 700 affected examples under the new definitions as the replacement evaluation sample, retaining labels for the other four categories.
Keep the 700 affected labels under old definitions and score all 3,000, postponing new definitions until next quarter's labeling.
Exclude all 700 affected examples and score only the other four categories' 2,300 examples; spend this week's 400-example capacity visually reviewing changed-category cases.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [new-definition scores this week], [400-label capacity], and [direct comparison for unchanged categories]. Anthropic recommends evaluation aligned with the actual task and specific, measurable criteria. Relabeling only affected categories reflects the changes while preserving other categories' labels for same-condition comparison with last quarter.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Maximizes label accuracy, but 3,000 exceeds this week's 400 capacity; changing unaffected labels also breaks direct historical comparison.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Meets all three conditions without new infrastructure. Affected-category evaluation shrinks from 700 to 400, increasing score uncertainty; the remaining 300 cannot be evaluated until relabeled.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Uses all labels and preserves comparisons, but scores affected categories under obsolete definitions.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Preserves direct comparison but produces no new-definition scores for the two changed categories.

**References**: [Define success criteria and build evaluations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests)

questions.title: Correcting stiff Claude responses through prompting
questions.prompt:
A Claude API support team's responses sound overly stiff. An internal guide describes the desired tone, but no model responses have legal approval yet; approval takes three weeks. Conditions:

- Implement **today**.
- **Do not put unapproved response wording in the prompt**.
- Tone must hold **in unlisted situations** as inquiry types expand.
- Current p95 latency is 2.3 seconds, with a **2.5-second limit**.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Add ten more "do not" prohibitions and emphasize each with "absolutely".
Have the team write five draft responses today and include them in `<example>` system-prompt examples.
Raise effort to a high setting to improve overall reasoning and response completeness.
State the desired tone and reason, such as "This customer is contacting us for the first time, so answer in friendly, plain language."

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [no unapproved wording] and [generalize to unlisted situations]. Anthropic recommends describing desired behavior rather than listing prohibitions, and explaining reasons so the model can generalize beyond rules. Stating tone and rationale can be implemented today without approved examples and applies to new situations.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Prohibition lists tend to focus on enumerated expressions and generalize poorly; they do not follow positive-instruction guidance.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Examples effectively guide tone but introduce wording before legal approval.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Adds reasoning latency without directly addressing tone; it cannot guarantee staying between the current 2.3 seconds and 2.5-second limit.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Available today, needs no approved wording, and generalizes. Descriptions may guide tone less precisely than examples, so add approved examples when available.

Also note: Prompt formatting influences output formatting; writing prompts in a style similar to the desired response can help.

**References**: [Prompting best practices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices)

questions.title: Splitting 4,000 logs without near-duplicate holdout leakage
questions.prompt:
A team creates tuning data from 4,000 production support conversations. About 25% are near-duplicates where the same customer rephrased the same issue repeatedly. Conditions:

- Holdout size must be **at least 400**.
- Holdout must reflect **the production distribution**.
- **No additional labeling staff**.
- Prevent **near-duplicate leakage between training and holdout**.

Which split is most appropriate?

options.text: Remove exact duplicate sentences only, then randomly split all data 90:10 into training and holdout.
Delete every holdout example resembling training data, shrinking the holdout accordingly.
Treat each group of near-duplicates about the same issue as one unit and place it entirely on one side.
Replace the holdout with 400 newly human-written questions.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [prevent near-duplicate leakage] and [reflect production]. OpenAI SFT guidance recommends separating a holdout from the same dataset before training, and fine-tuning best practices recommend train/test splitting. Near-duplicates spanning both sides can inflate holdout scores, a general leakage principle; the cited documentation does not prescribe a deduplication method. Group-based splitting prevents leakage while preserving production-log distribution.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Removing exact matches leaves rephrased near-duplicates that can cross the split and leak.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Prevents leakage but can shrink the holdout below 400, increasing score variability.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Meets all four conditions. Large groups can prevent an exact 90:10 ratio, and grouping requires a similarity criterion.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Prevents leakage but requires authoring staff and produces a distribution different from production.

Also note: Embedding similarity can form near-duplicate groups. Thresholds affect group size; inspect a sample manually.

**References**: [Supervised fine-tuning](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/supervised-fine-tuning) · [Fine-tuning best practices](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/fine-tuning-best-practices)

questions.title: Addressing a medical classifier with 70% labeler agreement
questions.prompt:
A team tuning medical-document classification has 5,000 labels but only 70% inter-labeler agreement. Conditions:

- Contractual target accuracy is **90% and cannot be negotiated this quarter**.
- Relabeling budget covers **500 examples**.
- Release is in **four weeks**.
- Labeler disagreement has been confirmed to **limit achievable model accuracy**.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Spend the entire 500-example budget labeling new cases and train on 5,500 examples.
Improve labeling guidelines and relabel 500 disputed examples.
Increase training epochs to fit the training data more closely.
First negotiate with the customer to lower contractual accuracy from 90% to 80%.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [70% agreement limits accuracy], [500-example relabeling budget], and [nonnegotiable target]. OpenAI fine-tuning best practices recommend checking annotator agreement, noting that inconsistent labels limit performance and smaller high-quality data can outperform larger low-quality data. Fixing criteria first and relabeling the most disputed cases spends the limited budget on the largest source of the ceiling.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: More labels under equally ambiguous guidelines do not improve agreement or resolve the obstacle to 90% accuracy.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Targets disagreement within the budget and deadline. Guideline work takes time, and if agreement remains insufficient afterward, 90% may remain unattainable and require renewed target discussion.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: More epochs are recommended when the model does not follow training data, but fitting noisy labels more closely does not raise the ceiling and may hurt holdout performance.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Potentially practical, but violates this quarter's nonnegotiable target.

Also note: Remeasuring agreement after relabeling helps assess feasibility before training.

**References**: [Fine-tuning best practices](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/fine-tuning-best-practices)

questions.title: Finding mismatches between training and inference formats
questions.prompt: A team auditing OpenAI tuning data compares training examples with production calls. Choose **two problematic cases** for tuning quality. (Existing customers also cannot create new tuning jobs from January 6, 2027; this tests data-audit principles.)

options.text: Training examples have no system prompt, but production requests include a consistent system prompt.
Training responses vary from 40 to 300 words, and production responses have a similar length distribution.
Training files and production calls use the same JSON response key names and order.
Some examples exceed token limits, so their final assistant responses are truncated mid-response during training.
Training questions contain typos, and production questions have a similar typo rate.

questions.explanation:
The decisive evidence is the training/production correspondence in each option. OpenAI recommends keeping examples in the same format used at inference. Examples exceeding context limits are truncated from the end and should be brought within limits.

- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: not a problem here)**: Similar production/training length distributions are appropriate.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: not a problem here)**: This is a properly matched format.

questions.title: Filtering 30,000 synthetic examples for a smaller model
questions.prompt:
A team will tune a small model on 30,000 large-model-generated responses. Over-limit training examples are truncated at the end. Current data:

- 6,000 examples (20%) are complex inquiries, matching their approximately 20% production share.
- About 15% (4,500) fall below the quality threshold, evenly distributed across types.
- About 8% (2,400) exceed token limits, **all complex inquiries**. Removing both low-quality and over-limit examples leaves about 23,000 (23,460), including about 3,060 complex examples (13%).
- Remaining large-model generation budget is **2,400 examples**.

Training requirements:

- Responses must be **complete to the end**.
- Complex inquiries must make up **at least 16%**.
- **At least 20,000** examples.
- Additional generation **at most 2,400**.

Which dataset construction is most appropriate?

options.text: Truncate over-limit examples and exclude only low-quality ones; train on all roughly 25,000 remaining examples.
Exclude over-limit and low-quality examples and use all roughly 23,000 remaining without rebalancing.
Randomly remove simple inquiries to reach 20% complex inquiries, training on all roughly 15,000 remaining without new generation.
Regenerate over-limit complex responses to be shorter but complete, quality-filter them, and add passing examples to the remaining roughly 23,000.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [complete responses], [complex share at least 16%], [at least 20,000 examples], and [generation at most 2,400]. OpenAI notes that over-limit examples are truncated from the end and prioritizes small high-quality datasets over large poor-quality ones. Distillation guidance recommends similar diversity in training and evaluation. Because over-limit examples concentrate in one type, simply removing them shifts training away from production.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Preserves size and complex share but teaches incomplete endings, violating completeness.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Preserves completeness and size, but a 13% complex share misses 16% and underrepresents common production inquiries.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Preserves share and completeness but falls to about 15,000, below 20,000.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Meets all four provided enough regenerated examples pass. If pass rate is p, complex share is (3,060 + 2,400p) / (23,460 + 2,400p); about 34% or higher exceeds 16%, and total size always exceeds 20,000. It uses the remaining generation budget, and shorter responses may lose information, requiring sample review.

Also note: Asking only for shorter responses can omit essential content. Reapply the same quality threshold and use only passing responses.

**References**: [Fine-tuning best practices](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/fine-tuning-best-practices) · [Distillation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/distillation)

questions.title: Ordering tuning-dataset preparation
questions.prompt:
A support team is preparing SFT data from production logs with many near-duplicate inquiries from the same customer. After training, it will compare against the base model on a holdout from the same dataset. Each step consumes the preceding step's output. Put these steps in dependency order.

- (1) Separate and freeze the holdout using groups after near-duplicate cleanup.
- (2) After length corrections/removals, compare the remaining training response-type distribution, including refusals, with expected inference distribution; adjust and finalize the training file.
- (3) Collect candidates from production logs and convert them to inference message format, including system instructions.
- (4) Find training examples that would exceed length limits and be truncated; correct or remove them.
- (5) Group repeated near-duplicate inquiries across all candidates and keep representatives only.

items.text: Separate and freeze the holdout using groups after near-duplicate cleanup.
After length corrections/removals, compare the remaining training response-type distribution, including refusals, with expected inference distribution; adjust and finalize the training file.
Collect candidates from production logs and convert them to inference message format, including system instructions.
Find training examples that would exceed length limits and be truncated; correct or remove them.
Group repeated near-duplicate inquiries across all candidates and keep representatives only.

questions.explanation:
The order follows output dependencies. Uniformly formatted candidates enable near-duplicate grouping; cleanup must precede splitting so the same inquiry does not span training and holdout. Length checks and distribution adjustment apply only to training, hence follow the split. Removing long examples changes distribution, so rebalancing comes last. OpenAI SFT guidance recommends a holdout from the same dataset with similar diversity. Best practices recommend inference-matched formats, warn that long examples are truncated, and note that excess refusal examples teach over-refusal.

| Order | Step | Dependency | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | (3) Collect and convert candidates | Starting set used by all later steps | Fine-tuning best practices: Iterating on data quality |
| 2 | (5) Clean near-duplicates | Requires the full candidate set from (3) | General leakage-prevention principle |
| 3 | (1) Separate holdout | Uses cleaned groups from (5) to avoid shared inquiries | Supervised fine-tuning: Evaluate the result |
| 4 | (4) Check length limits | Requires the training partition from (1) | Fine-tuning best practices: Token limits |
| 5 | (2) Rebalance and finalize | Uses training data after (4)'s removals/changes | Fine-tuning best practices: Iterating on data quality |

Also note: Delaying near-duplicate cleanup until after splitting can leave nearly identical holdout inquiries in training and inflate evaluation scores.

questions.title: Constructing and preprocessing preference pairs
questions.prompt: Which pair construction best satisfies [Requirement 1]?
questions.context:
> [Company overview] Raon Mobility wants to improve customer-support tone for its car-sharing service. Two ML engineers and six support-quality staff participate. Today is October 17, 2026.
>
> [Data status] There are 6,000 comparison pairs in which staff chose the better of two responses to the same inquiry. Each is a single-turn inquiry with two responses. Chosen responses average **2.4 times longer** than rejected responses. Independent judgments by two staff members agreed **74%** of the time. Refusals such as "Policy prevents us from doing that" comprise **18%** of chosen responses, versus about **4%** expected in production. About **3,900 pairs** have length ratios within 1.5; about **400** of these have a chosen refusal response.
>
> [Requirement 1] Finalize preference-training pairs. (1) Signals must come **only from responses staff actually reviewed**, without mixing in newly model-written answers. (2) Staff can provide **at most 500 additional judgments**. (3) Training must use **at least 3,000 pairs**. (4) Reduce the tendency for response length alone to predict selection.
>
> [Requirement 2] After the first training run, responses became longer and refusals increased. Budget permits **only one more training run**, with no additional staff judgments and **at least 3,000 training pairs**.
>
> [Reference] Training follows OpenAI-style DPO: single-turn text pairs with one preferred and one nonpreferred response. Another 300,000 English support logs from the same internal service are unrelated to this tone task. In a small prior experiment on the same data, raising `beta` reduced overall learned changes but barely changed verbosity or refusal share.

options.text: Use all 6,000 pairs and spend 500 additional judgments reassessing pairs where the two staff members disagreed.
Keep only about 3,900 pairs with length ratios within 1.5, and spend 500 judgments reassessing disputed pairs among them.
Have staff rewrite chosen responses in the approximately 2,100 high-length-ratio pairs to be shorter with the same content, then use all 6,000 pairs.
For each pair with a longer chosen response, have a model shorten it and replace the original chosen response, retaining all 6,000 pairs.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are the 2.4× length gap and 74% agreement in [Data status], plus conditions (1)–(4) in [Requirement 1]. OpenAI DPO uses single-turn text pairs with preferred/nonpreferred responses. Fine-tuning best practices warn that evaluator agreement can limit model performance. Strong correlation between length and selection can teach length as preference, a general ML principle. Removing high-ratio pairs addresses (4), the remaining 3,900 satisfy (3), and using 500 judgments on disputed pairs respects (2) while improving signal quality. The cost is fewer pairs and discarded tone information from large-length-gap examples.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Meets (1)–(3) but preserves high length ratios, violating (4).
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Meets all four. Pair count drops from 6,000 to 3,900, and 74% agreement improves only partially.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Human-authored responses satisfy (1) and (4), but rewriting 2,100 exceeds the 500-item allowance in (2).
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Fixes length, but generated variants were not reviewed by staff, violating (1).

Also note: The 1.5 ratio threshold is data-dependent; check retained count and length correlation when varying it.

**References**: [Direct preference optimization](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/direct-preference-optimization) · [Fine-tuning best practices › Iterating on data quality](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/fine-tuning-best-practices)

Raise `beta` to preserve more original-model behavior and rerun with unchanged data.
First run SFT on preferred responses to align tone, then DPO on the same data with unchanged settings.

questions.title: Which grader should migrate first before Evals shutdown?
questions.prompt:
Today is October 17, 2026. A team running regression evaluations on OpenAI Evals will migrate to its own evaluation code. Deprecation documentation says Evals becomes read-only on October 31, 2026, and its dashboard/API shut down on November 30, 2026. Migration conditions:

- Move graders **independently, one at a time**, before November 30, without needing other grader definitions.
- Make **no new model API calls during grading**.
- Produce **the same score for the same input**.

Which grader is most appropriate to migrate first?

options.text: Copy the internal `python` grader's `grade` function calculating field-level penalties and call it directly in local evaluation code.
Copy a `score_model` grader's prompt and 0–1 tone range and call the model from local evaluation code.
Copy the `multigrader` formula combining accuracy, tone, and length along with its component graders.
Reproduce a `text_similarity` grader's `cosine` comparison by calling an embedding model in local evaluation code.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [independent migration], [no new model calls], and [identical scores]. OpenAI documents `python` graders as network-free user code (`grade`), allowing deterministic migration into a function without model calls. `score_model` uses another model and does not allow changing temperature for reasoning models; `multigrader` combines other grader outputs; `text_similarity` cosine requires embeddings. The correct choice requires matching library versions used by the internal function.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: The simplest migration meeting all three conditions.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Requires model calls per grade and does not meet same-score determinism.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Requires migrating all component graders together, violating independence.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Requires embedding-model calls.

questions.title: Checking position bias in a pairwise judge
questions.prompt:
A team uses an LLM judge to compare two models' responses in pairs. Presentation order is randomized, yet the first response wins 62% of the time. Conditions:

- Only **100 human-expert labels** are available.
- Judge calls may increase to **at most twice** the current count.
- Produce **new comparison results within two days**.

Which approach best checks and reduces position bias?

options.text: Switch the judge to a smaller, cheaper model and rescore the same pairs in the same way.
Increase comparison pairs fivefold and score identically so bias disappears in the larger-sample average.
Score each pair in both orders; count a winner only if it wins both, otherwise record a tie.
Have experts score every pair directly, replacing LLM judgments with those results.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [62% first-position wins despite random order] and [twice the calls, 100 expert labels, two days]. Randomized order makes this a signal of position bias. OpenAI evaluation best practices discuss position and verbosity bias, recommending pairwise or pass/fail evaluation, length control, reasoning before grading, and the strongest model, scaling only after consistent agreement with humans. Swapping order and grading twice is a common diagnostic, not a technique explicitly prescribed by the cited document. It directly reveals bias within the two-call budget. Disagreements become ties, reducing resolution; a high disagreement rate still indicates judge-reliability problems.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: A cost measure, not a position-bias test. Guidance recommends starting with the strongest model, confirming human agreement, then optimizing.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: More samples do not average away systematic bias, and fivefold calls exceed the twofold cap.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Directly measures bias and removes its effect from decisions within twice the calls.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Avoids judge bias but exceeds 100 expert labels and two days.

**References**: [Evaluation best practices › Create and combine different types of evaluators](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evaluation-best-practices)

questions.title: Prioritizing and measuring conflicting success criteria
questions.prompt:
A Claude API customer-message classifier compares its current prompt with one adding 15 examples. Success criteria:

- **F1 at least 0.85** on 5,000 held-out examples.
- **99.5% nontoxic** classification-rationale responses.
- **95% of responses within 200 ms**, a contractual commitment.

Preliminary experiments show higher F1 but greater latency for the longer prompt. Experts can grade **200 examples**, and the deadline is **one week**. Which selection rule and measurement approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Treat latency and nontoxicity as gates and compare F1 among passing candidates. Compute F1 from exact label matches, measure latency in deployment configuration, and directly grade 200 examples with experts, treating their fraction as the overall nontoxicity rate.

Treat latency and nontoxicity as gates and compare F1 among passing candidates. Compute F1 from exact label matches, measure latency in deployment configuration, and grade all responses with a binary LLM grader validated against 200 expert labels.

Rank candidates by one weighted sum of all three criteria. Compute F1 from exact label matches, measure deployment latency, and grade all responses with a binary LLM grader validated against 200 expert labels.

Treat latency and nontoxicity as gates and compare F1 among passing candidates. Compute F1 from exact label matches, measure latency once in development, and grade all responses with an unvalidated binary LLM grader.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [95% within 200 ms or contractual breach], [200 expert labels/one week], and the F1/latency conflict. Anthropic recommends specific, measurable criteria and gives multidimensional examples combining F1, nontoxicity, and latency. Choose fast, reliable, scalable grading: code for exact matches, validated LLM grading before scaling, and limited human grading because it is slow and expensive. Contractual latency should be a gate, rejecting even high-F1 candidates that fail it. The tradeoff is using all 200 expert labels for grader validation, leaving none for other assessments such as rationale quality, and potentially discarding F1 gains because of latency.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Gates are appropriate, but one toxic-response difference among 200 moves the rate between 99.5% and 99.0%, making that sample insufficient to establish the threshold. Human grading cannot scale to all examples here.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Matches grading methods to criteria and treats commitments as gates.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Measurement fits, but a weighted sum allows other gains to offset a contractual latency failure.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Gates fit, but it scales an unvalidated toxicity grader and uses development latency that does not represent the deployment's 95th-percentile commitment.

**References**: [Define success criteria and build evaluations › Define success criteria](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests) · [Define success criteria and build evaluations › Grading methods](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests)

Include some very long inputs near processing limits.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Excludes edge cases and uses a uniform distribution, failing to represent production and difficult inputs.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Includes irrelevant or absent input.

questions.title: When target-task gains conflict with general-instruction regression
questions.prompt:
A team compares a small summary SFT model with its base using a summary-task holdout and a separate general-instruction regression set unrelated to summarization and never used for training. Scores are differences from base:

| Epoch checkpoint | Summary holdout | General-instruction regression |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | +3 | −6 |
| 2 | +5 | −8 |
| 3, final | +6 | −9 |

Launch requires at least +4 on summary and no worse than −3 on general instructions. Only one additional training run is available, and both evaluation sets must remain unused for training/tuning. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Launch the final checkpoint with the largest summary gain and monitor general instructions after launch.
Retrain on the same data for one epoch to reduce general-instruction regression.
Mix regression-set questions into training, retrain, and use that same set to verify regression is fixed.
Mix separately collected general-instruction examples into training, retrain, and use both evaluation sets only for comparison.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answer: {{option:D}}**

The conditions are summary gain at least +4, regression no worse than −3, one training run and untouched evaluation sets. OpenAI's SFT guide recommends separating holdout before training and comparing with base. Epoch checkpoints can help when performance initially improves then overfits, but none here meets both thresholds. Mixing general instructions to reduce forgetting is general ML practice, not a direct recommendation in the cited documentation; it is the only listed approach with a chance of meeting the constraints in one run. It costs another run, and the mixture could reduce summary gains below +4, requiring verification.

- {{option:A}} meets summary gain but −9 fails the −3 limit.
- {{option:B}} is contradicted by checkpoint 1: −6 still fails regression and +3 misses summary.
- {{option:C}} may reduce regression but training on the test set destroys its independence and violates the untouched-set condition.
- {{option:D}} targets regression in one run while preserving evaluation independence.

Have an LLM judge yes/no whether a response contains personal health information.
Calculate ROUGE-L from the longest common subsequence of candidate and reference summaries.
Normalize the output string and compare it exactly with the correct answer.

questions.title: Policies preventing evaluation-set contamination
questions.prompt: A team creates SFT data from production logs and fixes 400 separately selected log entries as its evaluation set. A larger model generates some synthetic training responses. Which TWO policies preserve evaluation-score reliability?

options.text: Because the evaluation set is small, add its questions to training and reevaluate on them afterward.
Improve the baseline prompt by adding low-scoring evaluation questions as system-prompt examples.
Exclude near-duplicate logs repeatedly submitted by the same customers as evaluation entries from training candidates.
Do not include evaluation questions in the larger model's prompt for synthetic training-response generation.
Since validation loss decreases during training, omit the holdout and evaluate on all training data.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answers: {{option:C}}, {{option:D}}**

Evaluation must use separate, untrained-on data. OpenAI's SFT guide says a pre-separated holdout acts as a control and should have similar diversity to training data. Evaluation questions or variants leaking into training or synthetic generation inflate scores and invalidate base comparisons. Near-duplicate removal is general ML practice that implements this separation.

- {{option:A}} directly trains on evaluation questions, destroying independence.
- {{option:B}} is not weight training but adapts the baseline prompt to the evaluation set and contaminates later comparisons on it.
- {{option:C}} prevents near-duplicate leakage.
- {{option:D}} prevents evaluation information entering through synthetic-data generation.
- {{option:E}} discards the recommended holdout and evaluates on learned data.

items.text: Longer responses winning more often in pairwise judgments may indicate bias, so controlling response length is preferable.
Validate consistent agreement between LLM and human judgments before scaling.
Keep the evaluation set permanently fixed to its initial questions and avoid adding new cases found in logs.
Rerun the same evaluation set after each prompt, model or configuration change to check regressions.

2. **Yes:** Verify consistent human agreement before scaling; uncalibrated scoring is an anti-pattern.
3. **No:** Find useful evaluation cases in logs and expand the dataset over time.

questions.title: Rollback thresholds and observation for a tuned-model canary
questions.prompt: A team plans a 5%-traffic canary for a tuned classifier. It must meet accuracy SLA relative to base, but labels arrive three days later; meet p95 latency SLA; tolerate zero safety regressions such as prohibited responses; and decide expansion within two days. Human review capacity is 200 cases daily. Which TWO rollback/observation designs are appropriate?

options.text: Before deployment, set numerical thresholds for automatic rollback on latency-SLA breach or one safety violation.
Keep observing at 5% until labels are confirmed after three days, then decide expansion.
Assign the 5% canary only to new customers and compare with the base model's all-customer results.
Before labels arrive, have humans review up to 200 daily disagreements between both models on identical requests to assess accuracy trends.
Since offline evaluation already checked safety, monitor only latency and accuracy in the canary.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answers: {{option:A}}, {{option:D}}**

Three-day labels versus a two-day decision, latency/zero-safety tolerance and 200 daily reviews determine the design. Canary controls are general MLOps practice implementing OpenAI's evaluation-per-change and production-monitoring principles. Predefined thresholds prevent shifting criteria during observation; human review of response disagreements provides a proxy trend while labels lag. Tradeoffs are false-positive automatic rollbacks and only estimated accuracy-SLA compliance before labels arrive.

- {{option:A}} predefines quantitative latency and safety rollback triggers.
- {{option:B}} obtains confirmed accuracy but violates the two-day decision deadline.
- {{option:C}} changes request distribution through new-customer-only assignment, preventing comparison with all-customer base results.
- {{option:D}} reviews same-request disagreements within capacity to estimate accuracy trends before labels.
- {{option:E}} omits production safety monitoring despite zero tolerated safety regressions.

**References**: [Evaluation best practices › Continuous evaluation and monitoring](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evaluation-best-practices) · [Evaluation best practices › Create and combine different types of evaluators](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evaluation-best-practices)

questions.title: Porting graders into a custom evaluation system
questions.prompt: A team must migrate two OpenAI Evals graders into custom code before retirement on November 30, 2026. One `python` grader embeds an internal glossary; Evals has no network access and a 256 kB code limit. The other is a reasoning-model `score_model` grader; `temperature` cannot be changed for that model, so identical inputs yield varying scores. Preserve direct comparability with historical scores, reduce score variability, finish before November 30, and keep grading cost within three times current. Which TWO designs are appropriate?

options.text: Replace `score_model`'s score definition with rules to eliminate model cost and append the new scores directly to history.
Keep the `python` grader's rules unchanged, move only its glossary to an external file, and load it from custom code.
Append migrated scores without validation and attribute differences from history to judge-model changes.
Keep the same `score_model` prompt and score range, grade each item three times, and use the median.
Delay migration until after Evals becomes read-only on October 31, 2026, and complete it all just before retirement.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answers: {{option:B}}, {{option:D}}**

Comparability, reduced variance, deadline and three-times cost limit matter. OpenAI documents that `python` graders run without network and require code below 256 kB, while reasoning-model `score_model` graders do not support temperature changes. Externalizing the glossary removes the packaging limit without changing score semantics. Repeating the same prompt/range and taking the median reduces variability within three-times cost. Repetition/median aggregation is general practice, not a technique expressly prescribed by the documentation. Its tradeoff is approximately tripling `score_model` cost, reaching the cap.

- {{option:A}} reduces cost but changes score meaning and breaks direct historical comparison.
- {{option:B}} preserves score definition and comparability during migration.
- {{option:C}} appends without verifying comparability, violating that requirement.
- {{option:D}} reduces variability within the cost cap.
- {{option:E}} raises deadline risk; Evals is read-only from October 31 and cannot run new evaluations then.

**References**: [Graders](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/graders) · [Deprecations › Evals platform](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/deprecations)

questions.title: Splitting 100,000 evaluation requests and retaining audit results
questions.prompt: A team processes 100,000 Gemini API evaluation requests in about 1.8 GB of input JSONL. Results must be retained for audit for 12 months, processing must cost half synchronous calls, and at 36 hours after submission an interim report must be possible from completed jobs even if others remain unfinished. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Split input into five 20,000-request files and five Batch jobs; download each completed job's results into internal storage.
Call synchronous `generateContent` in parallel for all 100,000 requests and store responses internally as they arrive.
Split input into five 20,000-request Batch jobs, leaving results in Gemini until audit.
Submit one input file as one Batch job and download results into internal storage when it finishes.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answer: {{option:A}}**

The conditions are 12-month retention, half cost and a 36-hour interim report. Gemini Batch costs 50% of standard rates and targets 24 hours. Jobs still queued/running after 48 hours expire with no retrievable results; the documentation recommends resubmission or smaller batches. Job creation is not idempotent, so repeating a request creates another job. Results are downloadable for six weeks by default and then permanently deleted. The 2 GB input-file limit permits this 1.8 GB input as one file.

| Plan | Processing | Violated condition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| {{option:A}} | Five jobs, immediate download of completions | None |
| {{option:B}} | Synchronous, internal storage | Half cost |
| {{option:C}} | Five jobs, Gemini storage | 12 months: deletion after six weeks |
| {{option:D}} | One job, internal storage | Interim reporting from completed jobs |

- {{option:A}} meets all three. Tradeoffs are managing five jobs, no guarantee of how many finish by 36 hours because 24 hours is only a target, and repeated processing time/cost when expired requests are resubmitted.
- {{option:B}} supports retention/reporting but pays full synchronous rates.
- {{option:C}} splits correctly at half cost but cannot answer a 12-month audit after six-week deletion.
- {{option:D}} meets cost/retention but offers no completed subset if its only job remains unfinished or expires.

**References**: [Batch API](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/batch-api)

questions.title: Constructing an embedding-replacement evaluation set
questions.prompt: Which evaluation-set design best meets Requirement 1?
questions.context:
> **Company overview:** Daehan Hospital provides clinicians embedding search over clinical guidelines, drug information and internal protocols. Three ML engineers maintain it. Today is October 17, 2026.
>
> **Existing environment:** Two million document chunks are indexed with the current 1024-dimensional model, stored as float32. Production logs contain about 120,000 queries monthly. There are 1,500 labeled queries previously used to tune the current model's adapter. Abbreviations and full terms are mixed, such as 'MI' and 'myocardial infarction', and many drug names are similar.
>
> **Requirement 1:** Build a replacement-model evaluation set. (1) Clinician time permits 400 correct-chunk labeling actions; independently labeling one query by two clinicians counts as two. (2) Represent the production-query distribution. (3) Separately assess hard cases: abbreviation/full-term variation and confusion among similar drug names. (4) Avoid contamination favoring the current model through its previous tuning queries. (5) Statistical review requires at least 260 general queries for overall recall, at least 100 hard cases for hard-case recall, and agreement checks on at least 40 queries selected from either group. Deadline: three weeks.
>
> **Requirement 2:** Select a model based on overall recall@20 ≥ 0.87, hard-case recall@20 ≥ current 0.61, query p95 retrieval latency ≤ 120 ms, float32 vector storage ≤ 12 GB, and $500 reindexing cost, increasable up to 10% with department-head approval. Candidate Y supports reduction to 1024 dimensions.
>
> | Model | Dimensions | Overall recall@20 | Hard-case recall@20 | p95 latency | Reindexing cost |
> | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
> | Current | 1024 | 0.82 | 0.61 | 80 ms | N/A |
> | X | 1024 | 0.88 | 0.55 | 95 ms | $450 |
> | Y | 2048 | 0.91 | 0.78 | 140 ms | $520 |
> | Y reduced to 1024 | 1024 | 0.89 | 0.74 | 105 ms | $520 |

options.text: Select 300 general queries and 100 hard cases, label each once and omit agreement checks. Stratify general queries by production-log type and exclude previous tuning queries.
Select 220 general queries and 140 hard cases, with 40 independently double-labeled for agreement. Stratify general queries by production-log type and exclude previous tuning queries.
Reuse 260 already-labeled previous tuning queries as general cases and spend the new budget on 360 hard cases, including 40 independently double-labeled.
Select 260 general queries and 100 hard cases, with 40 independently double-labeled for agreement. Stratify general queries by production-log type and exclude previous tuning queries.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answer: {{option:D}}**

Requirement 1 specifies 400 labeling actions, with double-labeling counting twice; production representation; separate hard-case analysis; no contamination; and minimums of 260 general, 100 hard and 40 agreement queries. Anthropic recommends real-task distributions and edge cases; Contextual Retrieval measures retrieval failures as 1 − recall@20, missing relevant documents among the top 20 chunks. The budget is exactly 260 + 100 + 40 extra agreement labels = 400. Tradeoffs are no spare budget to expand any category and a relatively wide uncertainty interval for overall recall from 260 general queries.

- {{option:A}} has sufficient general/hard cases but omits required agreement checks.
- {{option:B}} has ample hard cases and agreement checks but only 220 general queries, below 260 for overall recall.
- {{option:C}} contaminates evaluation in favor of the current model using its training queries and fails production representation.
- {{option:D}} meets all five requirements.

**References**: [Define success criteria and build evaluations › Eval design principles](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests) · [Introducing Contextual Retrieval › Evaluation](https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval)

questions.title: Monthly cost of a small tuned model versus a replacement base model
questions.prompt:
A team classifies inquiries using an OpenAI tuned model based on `gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14`, which retires with its base on January 14, 2027. Today is October 17, 2026. Use these hypothetical calculation prices, not actual pricing:

- One million monthly requests, each with 1,000 input and 200 output tokens.
- Replacement base: $1 per million input tokens, $4 per million output tokens.
- Current tuned monthly cost: 0.6 times replacement-base cost with the current prompt.
- Adding three examples multiplies input tokens by 2.5.
- Replacement without examples fails holdout accuracy; with three examples it passes.
- Monthly budget $4,000; operation must continue in 2027.

Which choice is most appropriate?

options.text: Continue the cheapest current tuned model throughout 2027.
Switch to the replacement base with a three-example prompt.
Switch to the replacement base with the current prompt and no examples.
Run both approaches until January 14, 2027, then turn off only the tuned model that day.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answer: {{option:B}}**

Continuing in 2027, accuracy and the $4,000 budget determine the choice. With the current prompt, replacement input is one billion tokens at $1/million = $1,000 and output is 200 million at $4/million = $800, totaling $1,800/month. Current tuning costs 0.6 × $1,800 = $1,080. Three examples raise input to $2,500 plus $800 output, totaling $3,300 within budget. Tuning can reduce token costs through shorter prompts, but tuned models retire with their base and cannot provide the ongoing 2027 path. The correct choice costs roughly three times the current monthly amount.

- {{option:A}} is cheapest but retires January 14, 2027.
- {{option:B}} meets accuracy, continued operation and budget.
- {{option:C}} costs $1,800 but fails accuracy.
- {{option:D}} increases coexistence costs without specifying the post-retirement path.

**References**: [Deprecations › Fine-tuned model shutdowns](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/deprecations) · [Model optimization › Fine-tune a model](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/model-optimization)

questions.title: Sequence for responding to OpenAI tuned-model and Evals retirement
questions.prompt: Today is October 17, 2026. A team uses tuned `ft-gpt-4.1-nano-2025-04-14` (retiring October 23, 2026) and `ft-gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14` (retiring with its base January 14, 2027). Regression evaluation uses OpenAI Evals, read-only October 31 and retired November 30, 2026. Each step consumes the preceding step's output. Arrange the steps by dependency.

items.text: Use migrated evaluations to compare current tuned models and replacements on the same set and finalize migration criteria.
Gradually switch calls to qualifying replacements, starting with earlier-deadline `ft-gpt-4.1-nano` uses.
Inspect call logs and inventory services calling both tuned models and their regression evaluation sets.
Confirm zero `ft-gpt-4.1-nano` calls, then migrate remaining `ft-gpt-4.1-mini` uses in the same way.
Download the inventoried evaluation sets, graders and historical scores from Evals and move them to custom evaluation code.

questions.explanation:
**Correct order: (3) → (5) → (1) → (2) → (4)**

Output dependencies determine this sequence. Identify services/models/sets before selecting assets to migrate; migrate assets before comparable evaluation; establish criteria before rollout. OpenAI lists nano retirement on October 23, Evals read-only on October 31 and retirement on November 30, with tuned models following base schedules. The tradeoff is the near nano deadline: practical execution must urgently overlap work across uses while preserving these dependencies.

| Order | Step | Dependency | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | (3) Inventory uses/sets | Establish what to migrate/change. | Fine-tuned model shutdowns |
| 2 | (5) Migrate evaluation assets | The inventory identifies assets. | Evals platform retirement |
| 3 | (1) Compare candidates/set criteria | Migrated sets/graders permit equal comparison. | Graders |
| 4 | (2) Roll out nano uses | Criteria select candidates; nano has the earlier deadline. | Fine-tuned model shutdowns |
| 5 | (4) Migrate mini uses | Reuse the approach after nano calls reach zero. | Fine-tuned model shutdowns |

Finish (5) before October 31 because read-only Evals cannot create new evaluations. Even existing customers cannot create new tuning jobs from January 6, 2027, so retraining is not an alternative.

questions.title: Warming a shared prefix before simultaneous morning traffic
questions.prompt:
A Claude API support service shares tool definitions and a roughly 40,000-token policy system prompt across all requests, with a cache breakpoint already at the system prompt's end. At 09:00, 300 agents send initial requests within seconds; the cache is empty overnight.

- p95 time to first response immediately after 09:00 must be at most five seconds; uncached requests take about eight seconds.
- Budget permits only one shared-prefix cache write daily.
- Production requests stream and force `tool_choice: any`; this cannot change.
- Nightly maintenance prohibits API calls before 08:55.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: At 08:57, prewarm the same prefix with `max_tokens: 0`, streaming off and `tool_choice` omitted.
At 09:00, send one request with production settings, wait for its response to start, then send the remaining 299.
At 09:00, send all 300 simultaneously with production settings and rely on later requests using the first arrival's cache.
From early morning, send the same prefix every four minutes with production settings to prevent expiration, continuing at 09:00.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answer: {{option:A}}**

The constraints are five-second p95 versus eight seconds uncached, one daily write, fixed streaming/`tool_choice: any`, and no calls before 08:55. Claude caching entries become available only after the first response starts; parallel requests must wait for that to hit. Prewarming with `max_tokens: 0` reads/writes the prefix and returns without output, charging normal cache-write rates if absent. Such requests reject `stream: true` or `tool_choice` values `any`/`tool`. Default TTL is five minutes, refreshed on use without additional charge. Changing `tool_choice` invalidates only message-level cache, leaving tools/system hits intact.

| Plan | Cache at 09:00 | Violation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| {{option:A}} | The 08:57 entry is available | None |
| {{option:B}} | Remaining requests hit after the first writes | Five-second p95: they wait about eight seconds |
| {{option:C}} | All arrive before the first response | One-write budget and five-second p95 |
| {{option:D}} | Kept warm overnight | No calls before 08:55 |

- {{option:A}} meets all four. Tradeoffs are scheduling the extra call, starting traffic before its 09:02 expiry, and all 300 falling back to uncached processing if prewarming fails.
- {{option:B}} writes once but delays 299 requests until the first uncached response starts after about eight seconds.
- {{option:C}} makes all 300 write before cache availability, exceeding budget and taking about eight seconds.
- {{option:D}} keeps the cache warm but violates the maintenance window.

**References**: [Prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching)

questions.title: Cache breakpoints for fixed examples, document context and conversation history
questions.prompt: A Claude API prompt contains fixed examples (20,000 tokens), document-specific context (5,000), then conversation history. All requests share the examples, but service-wide requests average 15 minutes apart. Document context is reused only within a roughly ten-minute consultation session, with turns one to two minutes apart. Tool calls grow history to dozens of blocks. With at most four breakpoints, minimize write cost while preserving hit rate. Which placement is most appropriate?

options.text: One-hour TTL after fixed examples, five-minute TTL after document context, and five-minute TTL at history end.
One-hour TTL after fixed examples and document context, and five-minute TTL at history end.
Five-minute TTL after fixed examples, document context and history.
One-hour TTL after fixed examples and five-minute TTL at history end, with no document-context breakpoint.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answer: {{option:A}}**

The conditions are 15-minute example reuse, ten-minute sessions with one-to-two-minute turns, dozens of blocks, and minimum write cost without lost hits. Claude's default five-minute cache writes cost 1.25 times base input, one-hour writes cost twice base, and reads cost 0.1 times or less depending on model. One-hour entries must precede five-minute entries. Each breakpoint looks back at most 20 positions. Fixed examples need one-hour TTL because five minutes expires between requests. Document context lasts adequately with refreshed five-minute TTL within sessions. Dozens of history blocks can put context beyond the 20-position lookback, requiring its own breakpoint. The tradeoff is using three breakpoints and expensive one-hour writes for examples.

- {{option:A}} preserves hits while controlling writes.
- {{option:B}} unnecessarily pays twice-base writes for ten-minute document sessions.
- {{option:C}} lets the 20,000-token examples expire each 15-minute interval, destroying hit rate and rewriting every request.
- {{option:D}} saves a breakpoint but can miss document context once history exceeds the 20-position search range.

**References**: [Prompt caching › Pricing, TTL and breakpoints](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching)

questions.title: Dimensions and cutover strategy for embedding migration
questions.prompt:
A team serves five million documents indexed with `gemini-embedding-001` at 3072 dimensions and is migrating to `gemini-embedding-2` to add video/PDFs to the same index, reducing dimensions to save storage.

- No search interruption during migration.
- Combined old/new float32 storage at most 95 GB during migration.
- Cut over only if evaluation recall@10 drops no more than one percentage point from current.
- The new index must use `gemini-embedding-2` for video/PDF support.

A 10,000-document pilot measured differences of −2.1 percentage points at 768 dimensions, −0.7 at 1536, and +0.3 at 3072. Which migration is most appropriate?

options.text: Embed all five million documents into a new 768-dimensional `gemini-embedding-2` index and cut over if recall@10 passes.
Embed all five million documents into a new 1536-dimensional `gemini-embedding-2` index and cut over if recall@10 passes.
Embed all five million documents into a new 3072-dimensional `gemini-embedding-2` index and cut over if recall@10 passes.
Truncate existing vectors to the first 1536 dimensions, normalize and store them, continuing `gemini-embedding-001` and checking recall@10.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answer: {{option:B}}**

No downtime, combined 95 GB, at most one-point recall loss and required `gemini-embedding-2` determine the choice. The models' spaces are incompatible, requiring full re-embedding. Both use MRL and recommend 768/1536/3072 dimensions; `gemini-embedding-2` automatically normalizes reduced dimensions, while `001` requires manual normalization. Building a parallel index preserves old-index service until cutover. Five million vectors need approximately 61.4 GB at 3072, 30.7 GB at 1536 and 15.4 GB at 768.

| Plan | New size | Combined size | Pilot recall change | Violation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| {{option:A}} | 15.4 GB | 76.8 GB | −2.1 points | At most one-point loss |
| {{option:B}} | 30.7 GB | 92.2 GB | −0.7 points | None |
| {{option:C}} | 61.4 GB | 122.9 GB | +0.3 points | 95 GB ceiling |
| {{option:D}} | 30.7 GB replacing existing | N/A | Unmeasured | Required new model |

- {{option:A}} minimizes storage but its 2.1-point loss fails quality.
- {{option:B}} meets all constraints and the migration objective. Tradeoffs are only 2.8 GB headroom below 95 GB and a −0.7-point pilot result close to the limit, requiring full-set confirmation.
- {{option:C}} has best recall but exceeds storage.
- {{option:D}} uses documented MRL reduction with manual `001` normalization but never migrates to the video/PDF-capable model.

During migration, replace `task_type` with consistent prefixes for queries/documents and embed both using the same model. The recall figures here are hypothetical pilot measurements.

**References**: [Embeddings](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/embeddings) · [Embeddings › Matryoshka Representation Learning](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/embeddings)

questions.title: When serving a tuned model beats a base model plus prompting
questions.prompt: A team is choosing between a tuned model and a base model plus prompting for classification. Assuming a platform that supports tuning, which TWO conditions favor tuned serving in cost and latency?

options.text: Policies and knowledge change weekly and answers must reflect those changes each week.
Every request includes thousands of tokens of fixed instructions/examples, with millions of calls monthly.
There are only hundreds of calls monthly and prompts are short.
Response format and tone must change flexibly for each task.
A narrow classification task previously handled by a large model is replaced by an evaluated small model.

questions.explanation:
**Correct answers: {{option:B}}, {{option:E}}**

OpenAI lists tuning benefits including shorter prompts with reduced token cost/latency, substitution of smaller/cheaper/faster models, and consistent formatting. Benefits grow with call volume and fixed-prompt length and persist when learned content does not change frequently.

- {{option:A}} calls for context such as retrieval rather than fixing changing knowledge in weights; weekly retraining adds operational burden.
- {{option:B}} reduces long fixed prompts and saves cost/latency across many calls.
- {{option:C}} offers too little prompt/volume savings to repay training costs.
- {{option:D}} conflicts with tuning's strength in stable formats and tone.
- {{option:E}} reduces unit cost/latency through a small model, with quality confirmed by evaluation.

OpenAI is phasing out its tuning platform, so this is a conceptual question. Check actual platform availability and base-model retirement schedules before adoption.

**References**: [Model optimization › Fine-tune a model](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/model-optimization) · [Optimizing LLM accuracy](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/optimizing-llm-accuracy)

questions.title: Matching an embedding to index dimensions
questions.prompt:
An internal vector index has 256 dimensions. Use OpenAI Python SDK to request a shorter output vector directly instead of truncating 3072 or 1536 dimensions. Choose a model trained to preserve semantic representation when shortened.

```python

client = OpenAI()
resp = client.embeddings.create(
    model=[A],
    input=chunks,
    [B]=256,
)
vectors = [d.embedding for d in resp.data]
print(len(vectors[0]))
```

Which values correctly fill [A] and [B]?

options.text: [A] = `text-embedding-ada-002`, [B] = `dimensions`
[A] = `text-embedding-3-small`, [B] = `dimensions`
[A] = `text-embedding-3-small`, [B] = `output_dimensionality`
[A] = `text-embedding-3-large`, [B] = `encoding_format`
[A] = `text-embedding-ada-002`, [B] = `output_dimensionality`

questions.explanation:
dimensions is supported for text-embedding-3 and later models. The cited guide recommends specifying it at creation for text-embedding-3-small or text-embedding-3-large.

{{option:A}} (Incorrect): ada-002 does not support dimensions.

{{option:B}} (Correct): Use text-embedding-3-small with dimensions.

from google.genai import types

guide:
As of the reference date, Google Agent Platform is the only one of the three providers offering new fine-tuning access. This exam therefore emphasizes deciding whether prompts, retrieval, or tuning will improve performance, rather than executing tuning alone.

### 1. Introduction

**Purpose**: This exam assesses whether candidates can diagnose model-performance issues and select and implement the best optimization path among prompt improvements, retrieval augmentation, embedding selection, and fine-tuning.

**Objectives**

- Distinguish missing-context problems from behavior/format problems and choose the appropriate optimization path.
- Select embedding models and settings that determine retrieval quality.
- Choose supervised, preference-based, or reinforcement-based tuning and prepare datasets for the goal.
- Compare base and tuned models on the same evaluation set.
- Manage serving cost and lifecycle implications of base-model retirement.

### 2. Target candidates

- ML engineers, data scientists, applied scientists, search and RAG engineers

**Recommended background and exam scope**

- Two years of ML engineering and ADA-level API knowledge are recommended.
- Pretraining and operating self-hosted open models are out of scope.

### 3. Content domains

| Domain | Weight |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Diagnosing and selecting optimization paths | 25% |
| 2. Embeddings and retrieval models | 20% |
| 3. Tuning methods and datasets | 25% |
| 4. Evaluation and comparison | 20% |
| 5. Serving and lifecycle | 10% |

**Domain 1: Diagnosing and selecting optimization paths**

- Knowledge: Two accuracy-optimization dimensions—context the model needs and how it behaves; problems solved by prompting, RAG, and tuning; current tuning availability across providers.
- Skills: Choose the lowest-cost path meeting goals for given failures and constraints such as data volume, budget, and current vendor.

**Domain 2: Embeddings and retrieval models**

- Knowledge: Dimensions, task types, multilingual and domain-specific embeddings, and provider-recommended models including external partners.
- Skills: Select models and dimensions for retrieval accuracy, storage cost, and latency requirements.

**Domain 3: Tuning methods and datasets**

- Knowledge: Supervised fine-tuning, DPO, reinforcement-based tuning, train/validation splits, data formats, and key hyperparameters.
- Skills: Select tuning for fixed formats, tone, or learned decision criteria; diagnose data-quality problems.

**Domain 4: Evaluation and comparison**

- Knowledge: Evaluation-set design, code and model grading, overfitting signals, and improvement over base models.
- Skills: Design comparisons that determine whether tuning genuinely improves performance.

**Domain 5: Serving and lifecycle**

- Knowledge: Tuned-model serving methods and costs, effects of base-model retirement, and alternatives when tuning services end.
- Skills: Compare total ownership costs of a tuned model versus a current base model with prompts.
